chapters.title: Python foundations: values, types and operators
chapters.summary: Names refer to objects, and each object has a type. Predict arithmetic, comparisons and truth values before writing transformations.
chapters.lesson:
Start with a tiny calculation and inspect both its value and its type. The expression 9 / 2 produces 4.5, while 9 // 2 produces 4. Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, which matters for negative values. Integers can grow beyond a fixed machine word, subject to memory limits; floating-point values approximate many decimal fractions.

A variable is a name referring to an object. Assigning another name does not automatically copy that object. Use == to compare values and is to compare identity. The usual missing-value marker is None; check it with is None. Empty containers, zero and None are false in a condition, but the string '0' is true because it is nonempty.

Conversions are explicit. int('12') succeeds; int('12.5') does not parse a decimal string directly. In a pipeline, distinguish missing data, an empty string and numeric zero rather than treating them as the same business event. Practice predicting an expression before running it, then explain any mismatch in your own words.
chapters.exercise: Create five values of different types; inspect their types and convert only valid integer strings.

chapters.title: Text processing and string operations
chapters.summary: Strings are immutable Unicode sequences. Use slicing, normalization and formatting deliberately when preparing data.
chapters.lesson:
Text arrives as identifiers, labels and values that still need parsing. Python str represents Unicode text. It is immutable: strip and replace return another string rather than editing the original object. Keep the returned value when you intend to clean data.

Indexing selects one character; slicing selects a range. The start is included and the stop excluded: 'batch'[1:4] gives 'atc'. Negative indices count from the end. An out-of-range slice stops at the boundary, but an out-of-range single index raises IndexError.

Use split for simple delimiters and join to assemble strings. split() without a separator treats whitespace runs differently from split(' '). strip('ab') removes listed characters from both edges, not one exact prefix; removeprefix expresses that different intent.

At system boundaries, encode converts text into bytes and decode does the reverse. Normalize according to business rules: casefold supports caseless matching, but changing a case-sensitive identifier can merge distinct records. An f-string formats output; it does not validate a value or make it safe for every downstream use.
chapters.exercise: Normalize city labels with strip and casefold while retaining each original label.

chapters.title: Lists, tuples, copying and unpacking
chapters.summary: Lists are mutable ordered collections; tuples have a fixed sequence of references. Understand aliasing before changing nested records.
chapters.lesson:
A list is an ordered, mutable sequence for an in-memory batch that may grow or change. A tuple is ordered too, but its element references cannot be replaced. A mutable object inside a tuple can still change, so tuple immutability is not deep immutability.

Assignment creates another reference. If b = a and a is a list, mutations through either name affect that list. a.copy() creates a new outer list while nested objects remain shared. For example, copying [[1]] does not automatically copy its inner list. Decide whether shared nested state is intended.

append adds one object; extend adds elements from an iterable. sort mutates a list and returns None; sorted builds a new list. Slices use an inclusive start and exclusive stop, and slice assignment can replace an entire region.

Unpacking assigns meaningful names to fields: key, value = pair expects exactly two elements. A starred target collects remaining elements into a list. Clear unpacking improves transformations, but an unexpected record length deserves validation. Practice explaining whether each operation changes an existing object, builds a new one, or merely rebinds a name.
chapters.exercise: Compare an alias, a shallow copy and independent nested lists by changing one inner element.

chapters.title: Dictionaries, sets and key semantics
chapters.summary: Dictionaries map unique hashable keys to values. Sets represent uniqueness and support reconciliation operations.
chapters.lesson:
A dictionary maps unique keys to values and suits counts, lookup tables and small configurations. Keys must be hashable: strings, integers and suitable tuples work, while lists do not. Assigning an existing key replaces its value. Iteration follows insertion order, but dictionary equality does not depend on that order.

Use d[key] when absence should raise KeyError, and d.get(key, default) when a fallback is intentional. A key whose value is None is still present. d.items() yields key-value pairs, and dictionary views reflect later changes rather than freezing a snapshot.

A set stores unique hashable elements. For identifier reconciliation, left & right finds shared IDs, left - right finds IDs only on the left, and left ^ right finds IDs present in exactly one set. Sets have no guaranteed iteration order or positional indexing.

Choose structures from their meaning. Deduplicating with a set discards order; list(dict.fromkeys(values)) preserves first-occurrence order. Also normalize identifier types: True and 1 compare equal as dictionary keys. Correct data modeling includes deciding what counts as the same key.
chapters.exercise: Reconcile source and target IDs using intersection, difference and symmetric difference.

chapters.title: Control flow and comprehensions
chapters.summary: Conditions choose a path, loops repeat work, and comprehensions build collections. Read the order of evaluation to predict a transformation.
chapters.lesson:
Start a transformation by stating the rule in ordinary language: keep only positive amounts, calculate a new value, then collect the results. An if statement chooses a branch. A for loop consumes an iterable; a while loop repeats while its condition is truthy. Ensure a while loop makes progress toward stopping.

range represents an arithmetic sequence without constructing a full list. Its stop is excluded. enumerate adds an index, and zip combines iterables positionally. In Python 3.11, zip stops at the shortest input unless strict=True asks it to reject unequal lengths.

A list comprehension expresses a mapping with an optional filter: [x * 2 for x in values if x > 0]. The final if filters existing inputs; a conditional expression before for chooses an output value. Multiple for clauses execute in the same nesting order as ordinary loops.

break exits the nearest loop and skips that loop's else block. continue skips the rest of the current iteration. A loop else runs on normal exhaustion, even for an empty input. For pipeline code, prefer clear control flow over compact expressions whose evaluation order is difficult to review.
chapters.exercise: Filter positive values, replace negative values with zero in a separate result, and explain why those are different transformations.

chapters.title: Functions, arguments and reusable transformations
chapters.summary: Functions package one operation behind a clear interface. Learn parameter rules and distinguish returning results from mutating inputs.
chapters.lesson:
A function gives a transformation a name and an interface. Define parameters with def, then supply arguments when calling it. A return statement ends the call and provides a result. Without an explicit return, the result is None; printing a value does not return it.

Arguments bind to local names that reference the supplied objects. Rebinding a parameter does not rebind the caller's name. Mutating a passed list can still affect the caller because both names refer to the same object. Make that behavior intentional and document it.

Default argument expressions run when the function is defined. A default list is therefore shared across calls. Prefer a None sentinel and create a fresh list inside the function. Positional-only parameters appear before /, and keyword-only parameters follow *. These markers make important API decisions explicit.

Use *args for additional positional arguments and **kwargs for additional keyword arguments. Unpacking at a call site reverses the process. Small functions with clear inputs and outputs are easier to reason about in an ETL pipeline. Prefer a specific transformation name and an explicit missing-value policy over a function that silently performs several unrelated steps.
chapters.exercise: Write normalize_label(text, *, lowercase=True), returning a new value without printing; then test several inputs interactively.

chapters.title: Scopes, closures and decorators
chapters.summary: Name lookup follows nested scopes, and closures retain access to enclosing bindings. Decorators compose behavior around functions.
chapters.lesson:
A name lookup usually searches local, enclosing-function, module-global and built-in scopes. Assignment inside a function makes that name local unless global or nonlocal declares otherwise. This explains why reading a name before a local assignment can raise UnboundLocalError even if a global with that name exists.

global targets the module namespace. nonlocal targets an existing enclosing-function binding. Neither declaration is needed merely to mutate an object referenced from an outer scope; rebinding and mutation are different operations.

A closure is a function that retains access to enclosing bindings after the outer call finishes. Closures normally look up a captured variable when called, not when created. Functions built in a loop can therefore all observe the loop's final value. A default argument can deliberately capture the current value when each function is defined.

A decorator accepts a callable and returns a replacement, often a wrapper. @decorate above a definition is equivalent to rebinding the function through decorate. A wrapper should usually forward *args and **kwargs, return the wrapped result, and use functools.wraps to preserve useful metadata. Understand these mechanics before applying decorators to retries, metrics or validation.
chapters.exercise: Build a multiplier factory and a decorator that preserves a wrapped function name and return value.

chapters.title: Iterators, generators and lazy processing
chapters.summary: Iterators produce one value at a time and remember consumption state. Generators make incremental transformations easier to express.
chapters.lesson:
An iterable can provide an iterator. An iterator remembers where it is and supplies the next value through next. A list can create fresh iterators repeatedly, but an iterator is usually a one-pass stream. After exhaustion, next raises StopIteration unless a default is supplied.

A function containing yield returns a generator when called. Its body starts when consumption begins and pauses at each yield. Local state remains available when execution resumes. A generator expression uses parentheses, such as (x * 2 for x in values), to compute results on demand.

Lazy processing can reduce peak memory when a pipeline consumes values incrementally. It does not help if the next step immediately calls list on the entire stream. Laziness also affects timing: errors and side effects inside a generator often occur during consumption, not creation.

The itertools module provides building blocks such as chain, islice and groupby. groupby groups adjacent equal keys rather than globally collecting all equal keys; sort first when that matches your desired grouping. Some tools retain state: tee may buffer data if its consumers progress unevenly. Understand each operation's consumption and storage behavior before applying it to large inputs.
chapters.exercise: Write a generator that yields normalized nonempty labels, consume two values, then consume the remainder and explain the state.

chapters.title: Exceptions and context managers
chapters.summary: Exceptions communicate failures, while cleanup must happen even on unsuccessful paths. Handle specific failures and preserve useful diagnostic context.
chapters.lesson:
An exception interrupts normal control flow and searches for a matching handler. Catch the narrowest failure that you can handle meaningfully. For example, invalid numeric text raises ValueError, while an inappropriate object type can raise TypeError. A broad catch that silently continues can hide a broken transformation.

A try statement can include except, else and finally. else runs only if the protected body completes without an exception. finally runs while leaving the construct, including ordinary returns and most exception paths, so it belongs around cleanup. A return inside finally can override a result or suppress a failure and is usually a poor design.

Use raise to signal an invalid operation. Inside a handler, a bare raise preserves the current exception. Raising a domain-specific exception from an original exception records the causal chain.

A context manager packages entry and exit behavior for with. __enter__ supplies the as value; __exit__ receives exception information and can suppress the exception by returning a truthy value. Usually cleanup should occur while failures still propagate. contextlib.contextmanager offers a generator-based form with exactly one yield; place cleanup in finally so it runs when the body fails.
chapters.exercise: Create a validation helper that raises ValueError for negative counts and a context manager that records entry and cleanup on both success and failure.

chapters.title: Objects, classes and dataclasses
chapters.summary: Classes combine data with related behavior. Distinguish instance state from class state and use dataclasses for explicit record models.
chapters.lesson:
A class defines a type, and each instance can hold its own state. Instance methods receive the instance as their first argument, conventionally named self. __init__ initializes a newly created instance; it is not the operation that allocates the object.

An instance attribute such as self.items belongs to that instance. A class attribute is shared through class lookup. Putting a mutable list on the class can accidentally share data across every instance. Create per-instance containers during initialization or use a dataclass field with default_factory.

Inheritance allows a subclass to extend or override behavior. super follows the method-resolution order and supports cooperative designs. Prefer composition when an object merely uses another component rather than being a specialized version of it.

Dataclasses generate common methods from annotated fields, reducing repetitive record code. The annotations describe fields but do not automatically validate runtime input types. frozen=True blocks ordinary field assignment; it does not recursively freeze nested objects. A property can expose a computed value or controlled assignment. Keep models focused: a simple record does not need a large class hierarchy, and validation rules should be explicit rather than assumed from a field annotation.
chapters.exercise: Create a Batch dataclass with a name and independent list of records; prove two instances do not share their list.

chapters.title: Modules, environments and type hints
chapters.summary: Modules organize reusable code, environments isolate dependencies, and annotations communicate contracts. Keep imports predictable and make runtime assumptions explicit.
chapters.lesson:
A module provides a namespace for related definitions. import math binds the module name, while from math import sqrt binds one exported object. Importing a module normally executes its top-level initialization on the first import in a process and then reuses the cached module. Keep expensive work and application execution out of import-time code.

Use if __name__ == '__main__' to distinguish direct execution from normal import. A package organizes modules into a hierarchy. Choose descriptive filenames; a local file named like a standard-library module can shadow the intended dependency and create confusing import failures.

A virtual environment isolates a project's installed packages. Create it with python -m venv .venv, and use that environment's interpreter when running or installing tools. Record dependencies so the environment can be recreated rather than copied as a folder.

Type hints describe expectations for readers and static analysis. list[str] describes a list of strings; str | None allows a missing value. Hints do not enforce runtime validation automatically. TypedDict describes dictionary shape, Protocol describes structural interfaces, and Any opts out of many checks. Use precise annotations where they clarify a transformation's inputs and outputs, while validating external data separately.
chapters.exercise: Create an importable transformations module with an annotated normalize function and a guarded demonstration entry point.

chapters.title: Collections and algorithmic thinking
chapters.summary: Choose containers and algorithms from the operations your pipeline needs. Counting, grouping, queues and ordered searches benefit from purpose-built tools.
chapters.lesson:
An algorithm is a sequence of steps, and its cost changes as data grows. Focus first on correctness, then ask what happens when the input becomes a hundred times larger. Repeated full scans and unnecessary materialization are common problems in small Python data jobs.

collections provides useful structures. Counter records frequencies, defaultdict creates missing values through a factory, and deque supports efficient operations at both ends. A dictionary is suitable for lookups; a list is suitable for positional access. Neither choice is universally best.

For a frequency table, Counter(['a', 'b', 'a']) records two a values and one b. For grouping, defaultdict(list) lets each key collect its own list. Be aware that subscription creates a missing default but get does not. Bounded deques can keep a rolling recent history.

heapq maintains a min-heap, useful when repeatedly selecting the smallest value or finding a small top-k set. bisect locates positions in sorted sequences, but inserting into a Python list still shifts elements. Separate search cost from update cost. Prefer clear, tested standard-library algorithms when they fit, and keep ordering assumptions explicit when merging already sorted streams.
chapters.exercise: Count labels with Counter, group records with defaultdict, and maintain only the three most recent events in a bounded deque.

chapters.title: Bounded-memory algorithms for data pipelines
chapters.summary: Choose algorithms that fit the size and arrival pattern of your data. Understand what lazy evaluation does and does not save.
chapters.lesson:
A pipeline may read one record at a time and still exhaust memory. The important question is how much state survives between records. An exact set of every distinct identifier grows with distinct cardinality. By contrast, a running count and sum use a fixed number of accumulators. A top-k heap stores only k candidates, although processing time still grows with input size.

Ordering changes what is possible. If records arrive sorted by customer, consecutive grouping can process one customer at a time. itertools.groupby does not collect every occurrence of a key from arbitrary input; it groups adjacent equal keys. Its groups also share the underlying iterator, so consume a group before advancing to the next. heapq.merge combines already sorted inputs lazily without a full global sort.

For parallel processing, design a summary that can be merged correctly. Carry a sum and count to compute an average, rather than averaging averages. Preserve enough information to handle empty partitions and missing values consistently. Validate both correctness and memory growth with adversarial fixtures: repeated keys, all-distinct keys, very large records, and a consumer that runs slower than the producer.
chapters.exercise: Build a bounded-memory top-20 extractor and a merge of three sorted event files. Acceptance criteria: results match a small reference implementation, input is consumed lazily, and measured peak memory stays approximately stable as record count grows with fixed record size.
objectives: Analyze state growth rather than only input iteration
Combine sorted streams without materializing them
Design mergeable aggregates with correct semantics

chapters.title: Concurrency, backpressure and resource ownership
chapters.summary: Coordinate work without hiding failures or exhausting resources. Treat cancellation and cleanup as normal execution paths.
chapters.lesson:
Concurrency is useful when work can overlap, but adding workers does not automatically produce a safe pipeline. Identify the bottleneck first: network waiting, Python CPU work, native-library computation, or the destination database. A bounded queue can slow a producer when consumers fall behind. A semaphore can limit active requests, but it does not prevent you from creating a million waiting tasks and retaining their arguments.

Structured task lifetimes help make failures visible. With asyncio.TaskGroup, child tasks belong to a scope, and failures trigger coordinated cleanup. Cancellation is a request delivered at suitable suspension points, not a mechanism that rolls back external side effects. A thread started with asyncio.to_thread can continue running after the awaiting task is cancelled. Design the worker's own stop checks when necessary.

Resource ownership should be explicit: the function that opens a connection should close it, or clearly transfer that responsibility. Context managers and ExitStack support cleanup even when later acquisition fails. Test timeouts, partial acquisition, one worker failing while others run, and a producer that outruns its consumers. A successful design bounds outstanding work, propagates meaningful exceptions, and leaves no orphaned resource after shutdown.
chapters.exercise: Build a bounded asynchronous producer/consumer pipeline with three workers. Acceptance criteria: queue size never exceeds the configured limit, failures reach the caller, cancelled work cleans up acquired resources, and shutdown completes under a documented timeout.
objectives: Bound both queued and active work
Choose threads, processes and async work deliberately

chapters.title: Typed, testable and measurable pipeline design
chapters.summary: Separate business transformations from side effects. Use contracts, adversarial tests and profiling to improve the right bottleneck.
chapters.lesson:
A maintainable pipeline separates decisions from effects. A pure transformation accepts records and returns validated values or explicit errors. A thin boundary layer reads input, writes output and manages retries. This separation lets you test business rules with small fixtures without repeatedly contacting storage or external services.

Type hints describe intended interfaces to people and static tools, but they are not automatic runtime validators. TypedDict does not reject a wrong incoming JSON type; NewType does not create a new runtime representation. Validate untrusted inputs at the boundary and use explicit domain objects only after validation. Even a frozen dataclass can refer to a mutable list, so decide whether deep immutability is actually required.

Tests should cover invariants such as conservation of accepted and rejected row counts, key uniqueness, stable ordering where promised, and replay behavior. Include empty input, malformed values, duplicate keys and partial failures. Profile representative workloads before optimizing: wall time, cumulative function time, Python allocations and process memory answer different questions. A faster microbenchmark does not prove a faster complete job if I/O, serialization or resource contention dominate. Record data size, runtime version and measurement conditions so another engineer can reproduce the result.
chapters.exercise: Refactor an ingestion script into a pure validator and an effectful writer. Acceptance criteria: typed interfaces, runtime boundary checks, tests for malformed and duplicate rows, injected writer failures, and a reproducible profile identifying the dominant cost.
objectives: Distinguish static type hints from runtime validation
Test boundaries and invariants rather than incidental structure
Interpret CPU and memory measurements carefully

chapters.title: NumPy foundations: arrays, shape and dtype
chapters.summary: Model numeric data as typed arrays with explicit dimensions. Learn to inspect shape and representation before transforming values.
chapters.lesson:
NumPy stores array values under one dtype, which describes how each element is represented. An ndarray also carries a shape, such as (1000, 4) for one thousand rows with four features. Its ndim is the number of axes, while size is the total number of elements. These are different questions: how many dimensions, how long each dimension is, and how much data exists.

Start with a small example: np.array([[2, 4], [6, 8]], dtype=np.int64). Inspect its shape, dtype and nbytes before applying operations. Specify a dtype when data crosses a storage or service boundary; platform defaults should not silently become your contract. A fixed-width integer can overflow, unlike Python's arbitrary-precision int. Floating-point values approximate many decimal fractions.

Use zeros, ones and full when every element needs an initial value. empty allocates without initializing numeric values, so reading it before filling is a bug. arange expresses a step and excludes its stop; linspace expresses a sample count and normally includes both endpoints. For ingestion, validate shape and dtype together before treating an array as a batch of records.
chapters.exercise: Create a 3-by-2 integer array of counts. Inspect ndim, shape, size, itemsize and nbytes; then convert it to float64 and explain the changed storage cost.
objectives: Distinguish shape, size and dimension count

chapters.title: Indexing, masks and shape-preserving selection
chapters.summary: Select records deliberately with positional indexes and Boolean masks. Distinguish a gathered copy from assignment into the original array.
chapters.lesson:
NumPy indexes refer to positions, not pandas-style row labels. For a two-dimensional array, a[row, column] selects one element. A slice such as a[:, 1:3] selects columns while retaining that axis. Selecting a single integer index removes an axis, so a[:, 1] and a[:, 1:2] have different shapes even when they refer to the same column values.

Boolean masks express record eligibility. For example, valid = (amount > 0) & np.isfinite(amount) combines two elementwise conditions. Parentheses matter because Python operator precedence does not infer your intention. Python and/or ask for scalar truth and are not replacements for array operators.

Basic slicing commonly creates views. Integer-array and Boolean-array selection are advanced indexing and return gathered copies. However, assigning directly into a[mask] changes a; it is not the same operation as changing a previously gathered result. For selecting a Cartesian product of rows and columns, np.ix_ makes intent clear. Always inspect selected shapes on a tiny example before applying an indexing expression to a production batch.
chapters.exercise: Build a 4-by-3 array. Select one column as both a vector and a two-dimensional array; then filter rows with a compound mask and compare direct assignment with modifying a gathered copy.

chapters.title: Broadcasting and vectorized transformations
chapters.summary: Replace compatible scalar loops with array operations. Predict shapes and temporary allocations before scaling an expression.
chapters.lesson:
Broadcasting lets compatible shapes participate in an elementwise operation. Compare dimensions from the right: each pair must be equal, or one must be one. Missing leading dimensions behave like length-one dimensions. For example, a batch shaped (100, 3) can subtract a feature mean shaped (3,), producing another (100, 3) array.

For row-specific adjustments, a vector shaped (100,) does not express a column of one value per row. Reshape it to (100, 1) so that it broadcasts across the three features. These distinctions are much easier to verify with a two-row example than after debugging a huge batch.

Vectorized does not mean free. Broadcasting usually avoids physically copying a smaller input, but the output and intermediate arrays can still be large. A pairwise difference between shapes (n, 1, d) and (1, m, d) can create n times m times d values. Chunk or reformulate work when that exceeds the memory budget. Prefer native ufuncs for supported elementwise operations; np.vectorize mainly offers convenient calling syntax and does not turn arbitrary Python code into compiled numerical code.
chapters.exercise: Normalize each feature of a small two-dimensional array with a vector of means. Then apply row weights with a[:, None] shape transformation and calculate the potential memory of a large pairwise result.
objectives: Avoid unnecessary tiled data and oversized temporaries

chapters.title: Axes, aggregation and numerical summaries
chapters.summary: Reduce the intended dimension without losing your shape model. Distinguish totals, cumulative results and location-based summaries.
chapters.lesson:
A reduction combines elements along selected axes. For a table-shaped array, axis=0 removes the row axis and usually produces one summary per column. axis=1 removes the column axis and produces one summary per row. This is easier to remember as the axis being collapsed than as a verbal rule about moving up or across. Without an axis, many reductions combine every element.

keepdims=True retains reduced axes with length one. For example, a.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True) has shape (rows, 1), so subtracting it from a centers each row through broadcasting. A cumulative operation such as cumsum preserves intermediate running totals instead of producing only the final sum.

Choose the numerical contract too. The accumulator dtype can matter for overflow or precision. mean of integer data normally uses floating-point arithmetic, but float32 inputs may need a float64 accumulator for a more accurate result. argmax returns a position, not the largest value; ties and empty inputs deserve deliberate handling. A production summary should also define whether missing and nonfinite values are rejected, ignored, or counted separately.
chapters.exercise: Use a 3-by-2 array of measurements to calculate column sums, row means and centered rows. Explain the output shape for each operation, then compare sum with cumsum.
objectives: Choose accumulator types and missing-value behavior
Separate arg indexes from aggregate values

chapters.title: Copies, views, reshaping and memory layout
chapters.summary: Understand which arrays share storage and when shape changes allocate. Make ownership and contiguity explicit at component boundaries.
chapters.lesson:
An ndarray combines element storage with metadata describing shape, dtype and strides. A view uses existing storage through different metadata, so writing through it can affect another array. A copy allocates independent element storage. Assignment such as b = a creates another reference to the same array object and is not either kind of data duplication.

Basic slicing often gives a strided view. Transposing a two-dimensional array usually changes how indexes map to storage without moving each value. A later reshape may be possible as a view or may require a copy; do not use reshape as a universal guarantee of memory sharing. flatten always returns a copy, whereas ravel copies only when necessary under its requested order.

For a numeric array, np.shares_memory(a, b) tests whether the arrays overlap in storage. A small slice can keep a large source allocation alive, so copying a long-lived small subset can sometimes reduce retained memory. At native-library boundaries, shape alone is insufficient: contiguity, dtype, byte order and writeability may all be part of the contract. Optimize based on measured allocations, while preserving clear mutation semantics.
chapters.exercise: Compare an alias, slice, copy, transpose, ravel result and flatten result from one numeric array. Record shape, strides, shares_memory and whether writing through each result changes the source.

chapters.title: Missing values, nonfinite data and safe arithmetic
chapters.summary: Make invalid-data policies explicit before numerical calculations. Use masks to separate missingness, infinities and valid measurements.
chapters.lesson:
A missing numerical observation is a business fact, not merely a troublesome arithmetic value. Floating arrays often use NaN as a marker, but NaN does not compare equal to itself. Use np.isnan to detect it. np.isfinite accepts ordinary finite numbers and rejects both NaN and positive or negative infinity. Decide whether each category means reject, quarantine, omit from a summary, or replace under a documented rule.

NaN-aware reductions can be useful, but they are not complete validation. nanmean ignores NaN values; it does not ignore infinity, and an all-NaN slice has no valid mean. Report valid counts with numerical summaries so an empty valid set cannot masquerade as a trustworthy result.

For division, initialize an output array and call np.divide(numerator, denominator, out=output, where=valid). Positions where valid is false retain the initialized output. This avoids evaluating forbidden divisions at those positions. In contrast, np.where(valid, numerator / denominator, fallback) evaluates the division expression first. errstate controls floating-error handling locally; suppressing a warning does not make the resulting values valid.
chapters.exercise: Create measurements containing finite numbers, NaN and infinity. Produce validity counts, an explicitly defined summary, and safe ratios with a chosen fallback for zero denominators.

chapters.title: pandas foundations: labeled tables and Series
chapters.summary: Model small and medium datasets as labeled columns. Inspect structure before changing values.
chapters.lesson:
A pandas DataFrame is a two-dimensional table with an index for rows and labels for columns. Each column is usually a Series with one dtype. Columns can have different dtypes, which makes a DataFrame useful for business records containing identifiers, amounts and timestamps. Unlike an ordinary list of lists, labels participate in many pandas operations.

Start by constructing a tiny table, inspecting shape, columns and dtypes, then choosing one column. For example, pd.DataFrame({'id': [10, 20], 'amount': [3, 7]}) has two rows and two columns. Selecting df['amount'] returns a Series; selecting df[['amount']] retains a DataFrame. The distinction affects later operations and return shapes.

The index is not automatically a primary key. It may contain duplicates, and it is not necessarily the physical row number. Data engineers should check uniqueness when labels represent business keys. A default RangeIndex is simply a convenient label sequence. Inspect the source schema and row grain before performing a transformation. A table of order lines is different from a table of orders, even when both contain an order_id column.
chapters.exercise: Create a five-row order-line DataFrame. Inspect shape, columns, dtypes and index uniqueness. Select amount as both a Series and a one-column DataFrame.
objectives: Inspect shape, index and column types
Choose explicit row and column labels

chapters.title: Selection, label alignment and safe assignment
chapters.summary: Separate position from label and make alignment intentional. Write selections that remain correct after sorting or filtering.
chapters.lesson:
pandas offers two important indexing languages. loc uses labels, while iloc uses integer positions. A row label of 10 is not necessarily the tenth row. Label slices with loc normally include both endpoints when the labels and ordering permit the slice; positional slices follow Python's exclusive-stop convention. Make this difference explicit in review and tests.

Labels also participate in arithmetic and assignment. Adding two Series aligns matching index labels rather than simply pairing their first elements. Assigning a Series into a DataFrame column similarly aligns on row labels. This is powerful for joining measurements by identity, but dangerous when you accidentally intended positional assignment. Converting to a NumPy array discards index labels and changes that contract.

For example, a mask based on df['amount'] > 0 selects positive rows. Combine vectorized conditions with & and |, and parenthesize each comparison. Python's scalar and/or operators do not define an elementwise truth value for a Series. To update selected rows, use a single statement such as df.loc[mask, 'status'] = 'valid'. Under pandas 3.0 Copy-on-Write, chained assignment does not update the original table reliably or correctly; one explicit indexer makes your target clear.
chapters.exercise: Create a table with nonconsecutive row labels, sort it, and compare loc with iloc. Assign a reversed-index Series to a new column and explain the alignment.

chapters.title: Dtypes, missing values and explicit data contracts
chapters.summary: Preserve meaning when values are absent or malformed. Distinguish data conversion from validation.
chapters.lesson:
A dtype is part of a data contract. A customer identifier is usually text even when it contains only digits, while an amount may need numeric operations. Missing values complicate that contract: NumPy integer dtypes cannot represent NaN, but pandas nullable Int64 can represent integers together with pd.NA. The capital I distinguishes that extension dtype from ordinary int64.

Use isna and notna to identify missing values. Equality is not a general missing-value test: NaN does not equal itself, and pd.NA propagates an unknown result through many operations. An empty string is also not automatically missing. Decide which source tokens mean missing before filling them.

For example, pd.to_numeric(values, errors='coerce') turns invalid numeric tokens into missing values. That is a conversion policy, not proof that the source was valid. Count and inspect newly missing values so corruption is not silently accepted. Similarly, fillna(0) is appropriate only when zero has the intended business meaning. An unknown sale amount and a zero-valued sale can lead to different downstream metrics. In pandas 3.0, inferred string data uses the dedicated str dtype; explicit dtype='string' retains the nullable StringDtype convention with pd.NA. Record which representation your pipeline expects.
chapters.exercise: Read text amounts with valid numbers, blanks and invalid tokens. Convert them, report rejected rows, and preserve an integer ID column with nullable Int64.
objectives: Use nullable and string dtypes deliberately

chapters.title: Vectorized text, parsing and datetime columns
chapters.summary: Clean values with column operations and explicit parsing rules. Preserve timezone meaning across pipeline boundaries.
chapters.lesson:
The str accessor applies text operations across a Series while respecting missing values. For example, s.str.strip().str.lower() can normalize a category column without a Python loop. Normalization should follow a business contract: removing whitespace from a code may be valid, while changing the case of a case-sensitive identifier may destroy information. Use regex=False when a pattern is intended literally.

Datetime parsing deserves the same care. pd.to_datetime converts supported input into datetime values. An explicit format documents the expected representation and helps detect inconsistent records. errors='coerce' turns invalid timestamps into NaT, which should be counted and reviewed instead of silently accepted. Once a column has datetime dtype, the dt accessor exposes fields such as year and day of week.

A timezone-naive timestamp has no timezone interpretation attached. tz_localize assigns a timezone interpretation to naive times, while tz_convert changes the representation of timezone-aware instants. Daylight-saving transitions can create ambiguous or nonexistent local times, so define those policies explicitly. Converting known UTC timestamps to another timezone preserves the instant. A data engineering pipeline should document whether timestamps denote instants, local business dates, or calendar periods before normalizing or aggregating them.
chapters.exercise: Normalize a nullable text status column, parse timestamps with a fixed format, quarantine invalid records, and convert aware UTC instants into a reporting timezone.
objectives: Use the str and dt accessors
Normalize text without hiding invalid input

chapters.title: Grouping, aggregation and row-level transformation
chapters.summary: Build summaries without confusing group results with row results. Keep null-key and category policies explicit.
chapters.lesson:
GroupBy follows a split, apply and combine model. The grouping keys define which rows belong together. Aggregation reduces each group into summary values, transformation produces values aligned back to the original rows, and filtration retains or removes whole groups according to a condition. Choose the operation from the required output grain rather than from familiarity with one method.

For example, df.groupby('customer')['amount'].sum() returns a total per customer. If every original row needs its customer's total, transform('sum') returns a same-length result that can be assigned directly. Repeating an aggregation and merging it back can work, but it adds another alignment and cardinality boundary to validate.

Missing data affects both grouping and reduction. groupby(dropna=False) includes missing-key groups; the default dropna=True excludes those key values. size counts rows, while count counts nonmissing values in a selected column. With categorical keys, observed controls whether unobserved categories participate; specify it explicitly when output shape is part of your contract. Built-in reductions are usually clearer and faster than Python callbacks. Finally, sort business timestamps before order-dependent operations such as shift or cumulative totals; grouping does not establish the intended event order for you.
chapters.exercise: Compute per-customer revenue, row-level revenue share, event counts and nonmissing amount counts. Include a missing customer key and compare explicit dropna policies.

chapters.title: Joins, concatenation and cardinality validation
chapters.summary: Combine tables without multiplying business facts accidentally. Make key uniqueness and unmatched rows observable.
chapters.lesson:
A merge matches rows using key values. Before merging, identify the grain of both inputs and the expected key relationship: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-one. If both sides have repeated keys, each matching combination appears, potentially multiplying amounts and increasing memory dramatically. The validate argument lets a merge check the relationship you expect instead of relying on a comment.

For example, an order-lines table can join a unique product dimension with validate='many_to_one'. This verifies uniqueness on the right, but it does not prove that every product key matched. Add indicator=True and inspect left_only records when missing dimension rows matter. Also note a key difference from ordinary SQL equality joins: pandas can match missing keys to missing keys. Decide explicitly whether those records should match or be quarantined.

concat serves a different purpose: it combines objects along an axis and aligns labels on the other axis. Row concatenation appends rows, while column concatenation aligns row labels. For many input chunks, collect the pieces and concatenate once when memory permits; repeatedly growing a DataFrame can copy substantial data. Validate row counts, uniqueness and aggregate totals at each combination boundary rather than assuming a successful operation means correct business output.
chapters.exercise: Join order lines to a product dimension using validate and indicator. Add a duplicate dimension key, an unmatched key and a missing key; explain each result.
objectives: Handle null keys and unmatched rows explicitly

chapters.title: Reshaping, duplicates and hierarchical indexes
chapters.summary: Move between wide and long representations without losing record identity. Distinguish reshaping from aggregation.
chapters.lesson:
A wide table stores different measurements in separate columns, while a long table stores a measurement name and value in rows. Neither shape is universally better. Choose a representation that preserves record identity and suits the next operation. melt converts selected value columns into rows while repeating identifier columns. pivot reverses a compatible long representation into columns, but it needs a unique value for each index/column pair.

When those pairs are duplicated, pivot_table can aggregate them using an explicit function. That is a change in data grain, not merely a cosmetic reshape. Specify the aggregation instead of accepting an accidental default, and reconcile row counts and totals afterward. Missing combinations can create missing cells even when the original values were all present.

A MultiIndex stores multiple label levels on one axis. It is useful for grouped results and hierarchical keys, but level names, ordering and uniqueness still require attention. set_index moves columns into the index; reset_index can move them back. explode expands list-like values into rows, duplicating the other columns. If an amount belongs to the original record, summing it after explode can overcount. Think through what each output row represents before using a reshape in a production pipeline.
chapters.exercise: Melt monthly sales into long form, pivot them back, then add duplicate month keys and compare pivot with explicit pivot_table aggregation. Explode item lists and check whether totals are duplicated.

chapters.title: Time series, resampling and leakage-safe windows
chapters.summary: Build time-based features with deliberate boundaries. Distinguish elapsed-time windows from fixed row counts.
chapters.lesson:
Time-series operations require an ordered time axis with a clear timezone interpretation. resample groups timestamps into time bins and applies an aggregation, such as hourly sums. asfreq instead changes the frequency of the index without performing a group aggregation. These operations answer different questions, particularly when several observations occur in one period or periods are missing.

Rolling windows calculate a statistic for each position. A window of three means three observations, while a time-based window such as '3D' includes records within an elapsed-time interval. Irregular data makes this distinction essential. min_periods controls how many observations are required before a value is returned. Specify boundaries and labeling when events exactly at a bin edge matter; defaults are not a substitute for a reporting contract.

For predictive features, a window that includes the current target or future events creates leakage. A common causal feature uses earlier observations, for example a grouped shift followed by an appropriately ordered rolling operation. Test this with a tiny timeline whose expected included rows are obvious. Also distinguish timestamps from periods: an instant lies on a timeline, while a period represents a calendar interval. For business reports, verify timezone, calendar and daylight-saving effects instead of assuming every local day has exactly twenty-four elapsed hours.
chapters.exercise: Create an irregular timestamped series. Compare rolling(3) with rolling("3D"), resample to daily sums, and build a feature that excludes the current observation.
objectives: Control window boundaries and minimum observations

chapters.title: Spark execution and the session
chapters.summary: Spark describes distributed computations before executing them. Learn how a session, driver, executors, jobs and partitions fit together.
chapters.lesson:
Start with an ordinary Python program: it reads values, calls functions and prints results. A Spark program adds distributed workers. Your driver builds a description of the work; executors perform tasks on pieces of the data called partitions. The cluster manager supplies resources, while Spark schedules the work within an application.

Create the SQL entry point with SparkSession.builder.appName("learning").getOrCreate(). A DataFrame represents named, typed columns distributed across partitions. Calling select or filter usually constructs another plan instead of immediately reading every row. Calling count, collect or a write operation requests a result and starts execution as needed. This separation is called lazy evaluation.

For example, spark.range(10).filter("id >= 7").count() returns 3. The filter describes which rows qualify; count requests the number. collect returns every result row to the driver, so reserve it for small learning examples. show displays a small sample, while printSchema describes column types.

A DataFrame has no guaranteed presentation order unless you request one. Think in rows and expressions rather than Python loops over a giant local list. Learn these boundaries first: they explain many interview questions about memory, parallelism and debugging.
chapters.exercise: Create spark.range(20), retain even IDs, select an ID multiplied by ten, and inspect both the schema and ordered results.
objectives: Create a session and inspect a DataFrame

chapters.title: Schemas, types and DataFrame creation
chapters.summary: A schema is a contract describing column names, types and nullability. Explicit schemas make small examples and production inputs easier to reason about.
chapters.lesson:
A DataFrame pairs rows with a schema. A schema records the names and types of fields, such as customer_id as a long and city as a string. Spark can infer types from some inputs, but inference is not the same as validating a stable business contract. Explicit types are especially helpful for empty datasets, all-null columns and repeatable file ingestion.

Build a schema with StructType containing StructField objects, or use a supported DDL string such as "id long, city string". A nullable flag says whether a field may contain null; it does not automatically invent a default value. Arrays and maps add separate nullability rules for their elements or values. DecimalType is useful when exact decimal precision matters, whereas DoubleType stores binary floating-point values.

For example, spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Pune"), (2, None)], "id long, city string") gives both rows the same column contract. Use df.schema to access the schema object and df.printSchema() to display it. Row values may be accessed by field name or position.

Do not assume that changing column names also changes data types. Cast values deliberately, and test invalid conversions under the configured SQL mode. A precise schema makes later transformations much easier to explain.
chapters.exercise: Create a two-column DataFrame with an explicit long/string schema, one null city, and an empty DataFrame with the same schema.
objectives: Map Python values to Spark types
Inspect and preserve nested schema information

chapters.title: Selecting, filtering and expressions
chapters.summary: Column expressions describe row-wise calculations inside Spark. Select, filter and withColumn compose those expressions into a query.
chapters.lesson:
A PySpark Column is an expression describing a value for each row, not a Python list containing those values. Import functions as F, then use F.col("amount") to reference a field and F.lit(10) for a constant. Arithmetic and comparisons produce more expressions. Spark evaluates them when the query runs.

select chooses output expressions. withColumn adds a field or replaces a field with the same name. Neither changes the original DataFrame. For example, df.withColumn("tax", F.col("amount") * F.lit(0.1)) creates a new plan with a calculated tax column. Use alias to give a selected expression a readable name.

filter keeps rows for which its predicate is true. Combine predicates with parenthesized &, | and ~ expressions. Python and, or and not try to evaluate truth in the driver and are unsuitable for Columns. A SQL predicate string is another supported form, such as df.filter("amount > 0 AND status = 'paid'").

Use when and otherwise for conditional results, and cast for intentional type conversion. Be careful with missing values: a comparison with null may produce an unknown result rather than true or false. Practice translating one business rule into one expression before composing a larger pipeline.
chapters.exercise: Add a discounted_amount column, filter paid positive orders, and select a renamed order ID plus a conditional size band.

chapters.title: Nulls, NaN and data cleaning
chapters.summary: Missing values and floating-point NaN are different concepts. Correct cleaning requires explicit rules rather than treating every unusual value as zero.
chapters.lesson:
SQL null means a value is unknown or absent. It is not the empty string, zero or floating-point NaN. Ordinary equality involving null usually produces an unknown result. Consequently, filtering with col == None is not the way to find missing values; use isNull or isNotNull. Null-safe equality, eqNullSafe, also considers two null operands equal.

SQL boolean logic has three outcomes: true, false and unknown. A filter keeps only true rows. For example, filtering amount > 0 removes rows with missing amounts as well as nonpositive amounts. If missing amounts should remain for review, include an explicit isNull branch.

Cleaning should encode a business decision. fillna can replace missing values in selected compatible columns; dropna can remove rows based on selected fields or a non-null threshold. coalesce chooses the first non-null expression. An empty string needs a separate rule, perhaps after trimming surrounding spaces.

Duplicates also need a definition. distinct compares whole rows. dropDuplicates on a key identifies duplicate keys but does not promise which differing payload survives. If the latest event must win, use an ordered window with a deterministic tie-breaker. Keep rejected records when they are useful for diagnosis rather than silently destroying evidence.
chapters.exercise: Create rows containing null, NaN, zero and an empty string. Write separate checks for each and explain which rows each cleaning rule removes.
objectives: Deduplicate with a deliberate row-selection rule

chapters.title: Strings, dates and timestamps
chapters.summary: Built-in functions normalize text and interpret date values within Spark. Parsing formats and time zones are part of the data contract.
chapters.lesson:
Text often carries structure that needs to become explicit columns. Use trim to remove surrounding spaces, lower or upper to normalize case, and split to create arrays from delimited content. Regular-expression functions are useful for extracting or replacing patterns, but a pattern should be tested on missing, malformed and unexpected values. substring uses a one-based starting position, unlike Python string slicing.

Dates and timestamps are different types. to_date parses a calendar date; to_timestamp interprets a date plus time. A format such as "yyyy-MM-dd" communicates the expected representation. date_format does the reverse kind of work: it formats a temporal value into a string. Keep actual date types for calendar calculations, rather than sorting arbitrary human-readable text.

For example, to_date(col("day_text"), "yyyy-MM-dd") can turn a source date string into DateType. date_add then advances by calendar days, while datediff(end, start) returns the day difference. add_months handles calendar-month arithmetic, including short months.

Timestamps require a time-zone policy. The session time zone can affect parsing and rendering of timestamp values. Declare whether source timestamps already include an offset or represent local wall-clock time. A clean pipeline documents this interpretation and tests boundaries such as midnight and month-end.
chapters.exercise: Normalize names with trim/lower, parse a date column, calculate the next day, and test an invalid date separately under your SQL mode.

chapters.title: Aggregations, grouping and pivoting
chapters.summary: Aggregations summarize many input rows into fewer output rows. Group keys, null handling and the chosen measure determine what the summary means.
chapters.lesson:
A groupBy defines the keys for a summary, and agg defines its measures. For example, orders.groupBy("customer_id").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total")) produces a total for each customer. A global aggregation uses df.agg without grouping keys and summarizes the full dataset.

Count carefully. count(*) counts rows, while count(column) excludes null values in that column. sum and avg also ignore null inputs, so their meaning depends on whether missing means unknown or a genuine zero. If every measure value is null, a sum is null rather than automatically zero. Distinct counts answer a different question from ordinary counts.

Use several aggregate expressions in one agg call when they describe the same grouping. A pivot turns category values into columns; supplying an explicit category list stabilizes the intended output and avoids discovering every distinct pivot value first. rollup creates hierarchical subtotals, while cube requests all combinations of grouping dimensions.

Collection aggregates need extra care. collect_list retains repeated values, whereas collect_set removes duplicates. Neither promises an order after distributed aggregation. If the array order matters, impose one deliberately. Always describe the business grain of the output: one row per customer, per day or per customer-day.
chapters.exercise: Summarize orders by customer with row count, non-null amount count, total and average; include duplicate and null amounts in your sample.
objectives: Choose row counts versus value counts
Reason about pivot, rollup and collection aggregates

chapters.title: Joins and set operations
chapters.summary: Joins connect related rows; set operations combine compatible row collections. Correct cardinality matters as much as choosing the right API.
chapters.lesson:
A join combines rows according to a relationship. An inner join returns matching pairs; a left outer join also preserves left rows without a match and fills right-side fields with null. A left semi join returns qualifying left rows without adding right columns. A left anti join returns left rows with no matching right row, making it useful for missing-reference checks.

Always inspect key cardinality. If a key appears twice on the left and three times on the right, an equality join produces six matching pairs for that key. A join does not automatically deduplicate a dimension table. Null keys also need thought: ordinary equality does not match null with null, while a deliberate null-safe condition can.

Use aliases in self-joins and qualify ambiguous field references. Joining on a shared column-name list produces one copy of those join keys. An explicit equality condition can leave both original key fields in the result.

Union appends compatible rows and retains duplicates; it is not a join. Plain union aligns columns by position. unionByName aligns by name, and allowMissingColumns can fill missing fields with null. Set operations such as intersect and subtract have distinct semantics, while their All variants preserve multiplicity where supported. Test these differences with tiny hand-calculated examples.
chapters.exercise: Build two small tables with duplicate and null keys. Predict row counts for inner, left, semi and anti joins before running them.
objectives: Choose inner, outer, semi and anti joins
Align schemas for union and set differences

chapters.title: Window functions and ordered analytics
chapters.summary: Windows calculate values across related rows while retaining row-level detail. Partition keys, ordering and frame boundaries jointly define the result.
chapters.lesson:
A grouped aggregation reduces rows, but a window calculation adds context to each row. Define a Window with partitionBy for related rows, orderBy for their sequence and, when needed, a frame describing which neighboring rows participate. Then apply a function with over(window_spec).

For example, a running total per customer can use Window.partitionBy("customer").orderBy("event_time", "event_id").rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow). Summing amount over that frame includes the current row and all earlier ordered rows for the same customer. A stable event_id breaks timestamp ties.

Ranking functions answer different questions. row_number assigns consecutive positions and is useful for choosing exactly one record. rank gives tied values the same rank and leaves gaps. dense_rank also shares ranks for ties but leaves no gaps. lag reads a preceding row and lead reads a following row in the specified ordering.

Frames require care. rowsBetween counts row positions, while rangeBetween compares ordering values. Duplicate ordering values can therefore make their results differ. A default ordered frame is not always the frame a business rule needs. Declare the frame when computing running totals or last values, and validate it using a tiny example with ties and missing values.
chapters.exercise: For three customers, compute a deterministic latest record, previous amount and running total. Include two equal timestamps to test the tie-breaker.

chapters.title: Arrays, maps, structs and JSON
chapters.summary: Nested types preserve relationships inside a row. Spark can transform these structures directly without collecting them into Python.
chapters.lesson:
Many event payloads are nested. A struct stores named fields, an array stores ordered elements and a map associates keys with values. These types are different from a string that happens to contain JSON. Parse JSON into a declared schema before relying on its nested fields.

For example, from_json(col("payload"), "id long, tags array<string>") creates a typed struct expression. You can then select payload.id or access tags. to_json converts a supported nested value back into JSON text. A schema describes what you expect; malformed input and unrecognized fields need an intentional handling policy.

Exploding changes row cardinality. explode creates a row for each collection element, so an array with three items creates three rows. For empty or null arrays, ordinary explode creates no rows. explode_outer retains a null-valued placeholder row. posexplode also returns element position, which is useful when order carries meaning.

Indexing conventions differ across APIs. Array getItem uses zero-based positions, while element_at uses one-based positions and accepts negative indices from the end. Higher-order functions such as transform and filter operate on array elements using Spark expressions. Prefer these expressions when they fit the rule, and always test null and empty collections separately.
chapters.exercise: Parse JSON orders containing item arrays, inspect nested fields, and compare explode with explode_outer on nonempty, empty and null arrays.
objectives: Access nested fields and array elements
Expand collections with the right explode semantics

chapters.title: Reading and writing data
chapters.summary: DataFrame readers and writers connect Spark plans to files and databases. Formats, schemas, parse modes and write modes determine the external contract.
chapters.lesson:
Spark readers turn external data into DataFrames. The format determines available options: CSV needs delimiter, header and quoting rules; JSON needs a record-boundary policy; Parquet stores typed columnar data. An explicit input schema avoids relying on accidental sample values to define a long-term contract.

For example, spark.read.option("header", True).schema("id long, amount decimal(10,2)").csv(path) declares how to interpret CSV fields. A header labels fields but does not itself infer numeric types. Test malformed records under the chosen parse mode and preserve enough context to diagnose failures.

Writers are actions. df.write.mode("append").parquet(path) adds data to a destination, while overwrite can replace existing output. A file write commonly creates a directory with multiple part files, not a single file named exactly like the path. partitionBy on the writer organizes output directories by column values; it is different from a window partition or an in-memory partition count.

JDBC connects to external databases using the appropriate driver. Parallel reads need deliberate partition settings, and connection concurrency must respect the database. Partition bounds determine split strides rather than serving as a general row filter. Design and test reads and writes against small disposable destinations before relying on them in a larger pipeline.
chapters.exercise: Write a tiny DataFrame as Parquet and CSV to separate scratch directories, read both back with explicit expectations, and compare their schemas.
objectives: Read CSV, JSON and Parquet deliberately
Choose write modes and output layout

chapters.title: RDDs, functions and shared variables
chapters.summary: RDDs expose lower-level distributed collections and function-based transformations. Understanding their execution model clarifies closures and worker-side behavior.
chapters.lesson:
An RDD is a distributed collection whose elements can be processed with Python functions. SparkContext.parallelize creates one from a small local collection. map emits one result per input element; flatMap emits zero or more results and flattens that level. filter keeps elements satisfying a predicate. These transformations remain lazy until an action requests output.

For example, sc.parallelize(["red blue", "blue"]).flatMap(lambda line: line.split()) produces three word elements. Mapping each word to (word, 1) creates a pair RDD, which can be summarized by reduceByKey using addition. The reduction must be suitable for distributed combination; associative and commutative operations are the easiest to reason about.

Python functions sent to workers include serialized captured state. Mutating an ordinary Python variable inside a task does not update the driver's original variable. Broadcast variables distribute a read-only value for reuse; accumulators support controlled aggregation of updates back to the driver. Neither is a general shared mutable dictionary.

Avoid treating executor side effects as exactly-once actions. Tasks can be retried, and printed output may appear in worker logs instead of the driver's console. Prefer returned data and explicit transformations for results. DataFrames are usually the first choice for structured analytics, but RDD knowledge helps explain Spark's lower-level behavior.
chapters.exercise: Implement a small word count with flatMap, map and reduceByKey, then compare map and flatMap outputs before the reduction.
objectives: Use map, flatMap and pair-RDD operations
Choose broadcast variables and accumulators appropriately

chapters.title: UDFs, pandas integration and testing
chapters.summary: User-defined functions extend Spark when built-in expressions are insufficient. Their types, null behavior and distributed dependencies must be explicit and tested.
chapters.lesson:
Start with Spark's built-in functions. They are visible to Spark's expression engine and often avoid crossing into Python for each value. When a rule needs custom Python logic, a scalar UDF wraps a Python function with a declared Spark return type. Handle null input deliberately and make returned values match that declaration.

A pandas UDF uses Arrow for data transfer and operates on pandas objects in batches. A scalar Series-to-Series pandas UDF must return the same number of values as it receives. This is different from applyInPandas, which processes grouped pandas DataFrames and can return a different number of rows subject to its declared schema. Large groups can still exhaust worker memory.

Arrow improves representation and transfer; it does not make toPandas distributed. A toPandas result still lives in driver memory. Required Python libraries must also be available where worker code executes, not merely installed in a notebook's driver environment.

Test transformations with small datasets covering normal values, nulls, duplicates, empty inputs and important type boundaries. PySpark 3.5 provides assertDataFrameEqual and assertSchemaEqual utilities. Compare row order only when the transformation promises an explicit order. Use sensible numeric tolerances for approximate floating-point results, and keep schemas as part of the tested contract.
chapters.exercise: Write a null-safe string UDF, compare it with an equivalent built-in expression, and test rows and schema with PySpark testing utilities.
objectives: Declare scalar and pandas UDF contracts
Distinguish Arrow transport from local collection

chapters.title: Diagnosing join correctness, skew and adaptive plans
chapters.summary: Treat a join as both a data contract and a distributed operation. Diagnose multiplication, missing matches and stragglers before changing configuration.
chapters.lesson:
Before tuning a slow join, establish what a correct result means. Is the right side unique on the join key? Should null keys match? Are all historical versions valid, or only the version effective at the fact's event time? A fast many-to-many join can still be the wrong computation. Measure unmatched keys, duplicate dimension keys and output cardinality before adjusting executor settings.

Then inspect the physical work. Shuffle partitions distribute keys, but a very frequent key can dominate one partition. Increasing the overall partition count may help ordinary partition sizes while leaving that hot key concentrated. Adaptive Query Execution can optimize supported skewed joins using runtime statistics, yet it does not repair a missing business predicate or remove a legitimate many-to-many output explosion.

Broadcasting changes data movement and memory pressure; it is not an unconditional improvement. Project and filter the candidate relation, inspect its effective size, and check whether the join type and predicate support the proposed strategy. Compare the final executed plan and task metrics with the original run. Report total runtime, shuffle volume, spill, tail-task time and correctness checks together so a local speedup does not hide an expensive downstream consequence.
chapters.exercise: Diagnose a fact/dimension join with duplicate history rows and one hot customer key. Acceptance criteria: prove correct temporal cardinality, quantify unmatched rows, compare baseline and tuned plans, and explain any remaining straggler without changing business semantics.
objectives: Verify join cardinality and null-key policy
Distinguish data skew from insufficient parallelism
Read final plans and compare measured trade-offs

chapters.title: Files, paths and CSV ingestion
chapters.summary: Read data incrementally and make file handling predictable. Treat paths, encodings and delimiters as part of the input contract.
chapters.lesson:
A file is a stream of bytes; text mode adds decoding so your program sees strings. Specify an encoding such as UTF-8 when the producer guarantees it. A with block closes the handle even when parsing fails. Iterating over a text file usually uses much less memory than reading the entire file at once. This matters when yesterday's small extract becomes a multi-gigabyte delivery.

CSV is a structured format, even though it looks simple. A comma inside a quoted field is data, not a column boundary. Use csv.reader or csv.DictReader instead of splitting lines. Open CSV files with newline='' so the csv module can handle record boundaries, including quoted multiline fields. The reader normally returns strings; conversion and validation remain your responsibility.

For example, iterate through DictReader and convert row['quantity'] with int inside a narrow error handler. Record the row number when conversion fails. Path objects make names and directory traversal clearer: Path('incoming') / 'sales.csv' joins components without hardcoding a separator. Always distinguish discovering a path from opening its contents, and test empty files, missing headers and malformed records.
chapters.exercise: Create a UTF-8 CSV with a quoted comma and a missing quantity. Read it with DictReader, validate quantity, and report rejected rows without loading the whole file.
objectives: Use context managers and explicit encodings
Distinguish path operations from file operations

chapters.title: JSON, serialization and regular expressions
chapters.summary: Decode structured messages and validate text deliberately. Keep parsing separate from trust and business validation.
chapters.lesson:
Serialization translates objects into a format another process can store or exchange. JSON supports objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Python maps these to dictionaries, lists, strings, numeric values, booleans and None. json.loads accepts a JSON string; json.load reads a file-like object. The corresponding dump functions go the other direction. JSON parsing proves that the syntax is readable, not that an event has the required fields or valid business values.

For example, decode a message, check that it is a dictionary, require an event_id string, and validate the amount before writing it. Keep payload size limits because valid input can still exhaust resources. Pickle is different: loading a pickle can execute code, so it is inappropriate for untrusted messages.

Regular expressions describe text patterns. re.search looks anywhere, re.match begins at the start, and re.fullmatch requires the entire string to match. For a field that must contain exactly six ASCII digits, use fullmatch with [0-9]{6}. Raw string literals reduce double escaping. Prefer clear patterns, named groups, and tests for rejected input; a clever expression that accepts the wrong records is not a successful validation rule.
chapters.exercise: Parse newline-delimited JSON events, require an event_id matching six ASCII digits, and collect separate syntax-error and validation-error counts.
objectives: Distinguish JSON strings from Python objects
Use regex matching and groups correctly

chapters.title: Time, decimals and validation
chapters.summary: Represent instants and money without hidden assumptions. Validate boundary cases before data reaches downstream tables.
chapters.lesson:
Data engineering bugs often arise from values that look reasonable but have different meanings. A naive datetime has no usable timezone context; an aware datetime can identify an instant. Converting an instant between zones uses astimezone. Replacing tzinfo merely attaches or replaces metadata and does not perform the same conversion. Store a clear timestamp contract and preserve the original zone when business rules need local calendar interpretation.

For example, an event received at midnight UTC may belong to the previous business day in another zone. Parse the timestamp, normalize it, and derive the business date using the intended zone. Use zoneinfo for IANA rules because fixed offsets cannot describe seasonal changes. Ambiguous local clock times require an explicit policy.

Binary floating point is useful for many measurements but does not represent most decimal fractions exactly. For currency, construct Decimal from the original text, such as Decimal('12.30'), and select a rounding rule when quantizing. Converting an existing float to Decimal preserves that float's approximation.

Validation should distinguish missing, malformed and out-of-range values. Check finite numbers, allowed precision, date ordering and domain limits. Keep rejected records and reasons so quality problems can be diagnosed instead of silently disappearing.
chapters.exercise: Validate transaction records containing an ISO timestamp, amount and quantity. Convert aware timestamps to UTC, quantize amounts to cents using an explicit rule, and reject nonfinite or negative values according to your contract.
objectives: Validate ranges and special numeric values

chapters.title: SQLite, SQL parameters and transactions
chapters.summary: Connect Python transformations to a relational database safely. Use transactions and constraints to make retries and failures predictable.
chapters.lesson:
A database connection manages a conversation with a database, and a cursor executes statements and retrieves results. Python's sqlite3 module follows the DB-API interface and stores data without a separate database server. It is useful for local applications, tests and small analytical tasks. SQL statements and values should stay separate: use a placeholder such as WHERE event_id = ? and pass the value in a tuple. String interpolation is not SQL parameter binding.

A transaction groups changes into one commit or rollback boundary. For example, insert an order and its line items in one transaction so a partial failure does not publish half an order. In Python 3.11 sqlite3, connection context managers commit or roll back an open transaction on exit; they do not close the connection. Understand isolation_level and avoid assuming that closing a handle automatically commits.

Constraints let the database enforce facts even when multiple code paths write data. A unique event key can prevent duplicate ingestion, while a NOT NULL rule can reject incomplete rows. Use explicit conflict behavior and test reruns. Keep transactions reasonably short, check failure paths, and distinguish database guarantees from assumptions in application code.
chapters.exercise: Build a temporary SQLite order table with a unique event_id. Insert a batch using bound parameters, deliberately fail midway, verify rollback, then implement and test duplicate-safe replay.
objectives: Design keys and constraints for reliable ingestion

chapters.title: Logging, tests and diagnosis
chapters.summary: Make pipeline behavior observable and changes testable. Verify results and failure paths with small, purposeful examples.
chapters.lesson:
A working pipeline needs evidence about what it processed, what it rejected and where it failed. Logging provides levels, handlers and formatting so applications can route that evidence consistently. A module typically obtains a logger with logging.getLogger(__name__). Include useful context such as a run identifier and row counts, but avoid recording credentials or entire sensitive payloads. Logging an exception inside an exception handler preserves its traceback.

Tests should verify contracts. For a parser, test valid input, missing fields, malformed numbers and empty files. For a transformation, a tiny dataset with carefully chosen edge cases is more informative than thousands of random rows without expected outputs. Keep pure transformation functions separate from file and network access to simplify these tests.

Mocks replace selected external dependencies. Patch the name where the code under test looks it up, not merely where the original function was defined.
