Use realistic return values and assert meaningful interactions, such as the retry limit or transaction rollback. A test that duplicates the implementation can pass while preserving the same bug.

When a failure occurs, read the traceback from the failing operation outward, preserve the original exception context, and reproduce the smallest problematic input before changing multiple settings.
chapters.exercise: Write unittest cases for a record parser. Include malformed input, assert the expected exception type, capture a rejection log, and mock a storage call to prove invalid rows are never written.
objectives: Use contextual logs without exposing secrets
Mock external boundaries at their lookup location

chapters.title: Concurrency, async work and retries
chapters.summary: Overlap waiting without losing control of failures or resource usage. Design retries around operation side effects.
chapters.lesson:
Concurrency means multiple tasks can make progress during the same period; parallelism means work executes simultaneously. Threads are often useful for waiting on network or file operations. In conventional CPython 3.11, the GIL limits simultaneous execution of Python bytecode in threads, so CPU-heavy pure Python work may benefit from processes. Processes add startup, serialization and communication costs.

Asyncio uses cooperative scheduling. A coroutine gives other tasks a chance to run when it awaits an operation that suspends. A blocking call such as time.sleep inside a coroutine blocks its event-loop thread. Use asynchronous APIs or move suitable blocking work to a thread. Bound the number of concurrent requests with a semaphore or worker pool so a faster producer does not exhaust memory or overwhelm a service.

Failures must remain visible. Retrieving a Future result propagates the task's exception; merely submitting work does not prove success. Timeouts, cancellation and shutdown need explicit handling.

Retries should target transient failures and have attempt or time limits. Add backoff and jitter when many workers may retry together. A timeout does not prove the remote operation failed: it may have committed before the response was lost. Use idempotency keys or reconciliation before repeating side effects.
chapters.exercise: Implement a bounded worker pool around a fake unreliable fetcher. Test success, timeout and permanent failure, then add a retry budget and verify that a repeated write uses the same idempotency key.
objectives: Choose threads, processes or async tasks deliberately
Propagate task errors and bound concurrency
Make retries timed, bounded and idempotent

chapters.title: Spark execution plans and shuffles
chapters.summary: Read the plan behind a DataFrame transformation. Use evidence to distinguish expensive data movement from ordinary expression evaluation.
chapters.lesson:
A PySpark DataFrame is a description of a distributed computation. Transformations such as select and filter create new plans rather than immediately producing all output rows. Actions such as count or writing results cause Spark to execute the required computation. This lazy model allows the optimizer to rearrange compatible operations, remove unused columns and choose execution strategies.

Use explain to inspect the plan. A logical plan describes the intended relational operations; a physical plan describes execution choices such as scans, aggregates, exchanges and join algorithms. An Exchange often indicates redistribution, though broadcast exchanges and shuffle exchanges have different roles. Do not count Python method calls and assume each one becomes a job or stage.

For example, a filter on a partition column may let Spark skip directories, while a selected subset of Parquet columns can reduce the data read. A compatible data-source filter may be pushed down, but support depends on the source and expression. Inspect the scan details rather than assume all filters have identical effects.

Built-in expressions usually give the optimizer more information than opaque Python UDFs. Measure complete actions on representative data, because constructing a lazy DataFrame is not a benchmark of executing it. Compare plans and metrics before and after each change.
chapters.exercise: Build a filtered aggregation over Parquet. Inspect formatted and extended plans, identify scan columns and exchanges, then compare measured execution with and without an early projection.
objectives: Reason about optimizer visibility and recomputation

chapters.title: Partitioning, skew and adaptive joins
chapters.summary: Distribute work according to data size and key distribution. Tune joins and partition counts with measured constraints.
chapters.lesson:
A partition is a unit of distributed data and task scheduling. Too few partitions can leave cores idle or create oversized tasks; too many can spend time on scheduling and small-file overhead. Repartition redistributes data, while coalesce commonly reduces partition count through a narrow dependency. A drastic coalesce can concentrate work on too few executors. Choose based on the stage and output requirements, not a universal magic number.

Skew occurs when some partitions contain much more work than others. A frequent key can make one join or aggregation task dominate runtime. Adding ordinary hash partitions does not necessarily split that key. Diagnose key frequencies and task-size distributions first. Remedies may include pre-aggregation, isolating hot keys, carefully designed salting, or adaptive skew handling.

Broadcast joins distribute a sufficiently small relation to workers so the other side may avoid a join shuffle. The broadcast relation must fit the relevant memory budgets; compressed file size is not the same as its runtime representation. Hints guide planning but do not make unsupported joins valid.

Adaptive Query Execution uses runtime statistics for eligible changes such as coalescing shuffle partitions or changing join strategies. It improves many workloads, but it does not remove the need for good schemas, representative tests and memory-aware design.
chapters.exercise: Create a skewed join dataset with one frequent key. Compare task durations and plans for a baseline join, a safe broadcast dimension, and AQE. Explain which change addresses the measured bottleneck.
objectives: Recognize skew and choose targeted remedies
Understand broadcast joins and AQE tradeoffs

chapters.title: Caching, memory and performance diagnosis
chapters.summary: Reuse expensive results intentionally and identify resource bottlenecks. Separate driver limits from executor limits before changing settings.
chapters.lesson:
Caching stores computed partitions for reuse; it does not make every transformation faster. Persisting an expensive intermediate can help when multiple later actions reuse it, but storage, serialization and eviction have costs. Persistence is generally lazy: computation populates the cache when an action requests the data. Unpersist results that are no longer useful so other work can use the resources.

The driver coordinates the application and holds objects returned to Python. Calling collect or toPandas on an unbounded result can exhaust driver memory even when executor memory is plentiful. Arrow may improve transfer efficiency but does not make the final pandas object distributed. Prefer distributed aggregation or bounded inspection when possible.

Executors need memory for task execution, shuffles, cached data and runtime overhead. Spill means some intermediate data has moved to disk; it can be a normal safety mechanism, but heavy spill may reveal oversized partitions or insufficient resources. High garbage-collection time suggests allocation or memory pressure rather than useful computation.

For example, investigate a slow aggregation by comparing task duration, input size, shuffle bytes, spill and GC. Change one hypothesis-driven setting at a time. A benchmark should include representative data, cold and warm conditions where relevant, and the complete result-producing action.
chapters.exercise: Run two actions against an expensive intermediate with and without persistence. Inspect storage and stage metrics, then deliberately compare a bounded take with collect on a safe small fixture to explain driver-memory behavior.
objectives: Interpret spill, GC and task metrics

chapters.title: Structured Streaming foundations
chapters.summary: Understand event time, recovery and streaming output. Build a clear model before tuning a live pipeline.
chapters.lesson:
A streaming DataFrame describes a computation over data that continues to arrive. Create one with spark.readStream, apply supported transformations, then start an output query with writeStream. The running StreamingQuery is distinct from the DataFrame that describes the computation.

Event time records when an event happened. Processing time records when the system handles it. A delayed event can arrive after newer events, so event-time windows need a lateness policy. Watermarks help supported stateful operations decide when old state can be retired. They advance from observed event-time progress, not simply from a clock on the wall. The guarantee for late data is one-sided: sufficiently recent data will not be dropped by that policy, while older data may or may not be processed.

Recovery is part of normal operation. Give each query its own durable checkpoint and understand the source and sink guarantees. A foreachBatch callback can be repeated after failure, so external writes must tolerate replay. For example, store a durable batch identifier in the same database transaction as the batch output when the sink design supports this approach.
chapters.exercise: Sketch a stream of orders with source timestamps and delayed arrivals. Identify event-time windows, a lateness policy, checkpoint ownership, and how repeated writes would be deduplicated.
objectives: Distinguish event time and processing time

questions.prompt: What does the true-division expression print?
questions.code: print(7 / 2)
questions.explanation: / performs true division, so dividing integers can produce a float.

questions.prompt: What does floor division print for a negative numerator?
questions.code: print(-7 // 3)
questions.explanation: Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero.

questions.prompt: What remainder is printed with a positive divisor?
questions.code: print(-7 % 3)
questions.explanation: The remainder has the divisor's sign and satisfies a == (a // b) * b + a % b.

questions.prompt: What does exponentiation precedence produce here?
questions.code: print(-2 ** 2)
questions.explanation: Exponentiation binds more tightly than unary minus on its left: this is -(2 ** 2).

questions.prompt: What does the chained comparison print?
questions.code: print(1 < 3 < 5)
questions.explanation: Both adjacent comparisons must hold; the middle expression is evaluated once.

questions.prompt: What does converting the nonempty string '0' to bool print?
questions.code: print(bool('0'))
questions.explanation: Any nonempty string is truthy; its characters are not converted numerically.

questions.prompt: What does converting this negative float to int print?
questions.code: print(int(-2.9))
questions.explanation: int truncates the fractional part toward zero.

questions.prompt: Which exception does conversion of this decimal-form string raise?
questions.code: print(int('12.5'))
questions.explanation: int parses an integer-form string, not a string containing a decimal point.

questions.prompt: What does or return when the left operand is empty?
questions.code: print('' or 'backup')
questions.explanation: or returns an operand, choosing the right one when the left is falsey.

questions.prompt: What does and return when its left operand is zero?
questions.code: print(0 and 9)
questions.explanation: and short-circuits and returns the falsey left operand unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does checking True against int print?
questions.code: print(isinstance(True, int))
questions.explanation: bool is a subclass of int.

questions.prompt: What does summing Boolean flags produce?
questions.code: print(sum([True, False, True]))
questions.explanation: True behaves as 1 and False as 0 in arithmetic.

questions.prompt: What does rebinding a numeric variable leave in its old alias?
questions.code:
a = 5
b = a
a += 1
print(b)
questions.explanation: Rebinding a does not rebind b, which still refers to the previous immutable value.

questions.prompt: What does short-circuit evaluation print without dividing by zero?
questions.code: print(False and (1 / 0))
questions.explanation: The right side of and is skipped when the left side is falsey.

questions.prompt: Which literal conventionally represents an absent value?
questions.explanation: None is Python's singleton for absence; NaN is a floating-point value.

questions.prompt: Which comparison should check whether a value is None?
questions.explanation: is None tests the singleton's identity without invoking custom equality.

questions.prompt: What does Python's dynamic typing mean?
choices: Names may refer to objects of different types over time
Each name requires one fixed declared type
Every type error is caught before execution
questions.explanation: Types belong to objects, and a name can be rebound.

questions.prompt: Which expression converts a digit string into an integer?
questions.explanation: int parses a valid integer string; the others produce different types.

questions.prompt: What type does the literal 3.0 have?
questions.explanation: The decimal point makes this a built-in float despite its integral mathematical value.

questions.prompt: Why can 0.1 + 0.2 differ slightly from 0.3?
choices: Many decimal fractions lack exact binary float representations
Float addition first converts to integers
questions.explanation: Binary floating-point approximation can introduce rounding differences.

questions.prompt: Which operator compares values for equality?
questions.explanation: == compares equality; = assigns and is compares identity.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes is from ==?
questions.explanation: Separate objects may compare equal while having different identities.

questions.prompt: A pipeline receives '', 0 and None. Why distinguish them?
choices: Only None can be stored in containers
They can have different business meanings despite being falsey
questions.explanation: Truthiness groups values together but does not establish missing-data semantics.

questions.prompt: Which expression checks container membership?
questions.explanation: in invokes membership; is tests identity.

questions.prompt: Which operator raises a value to a power?
questions.explanation: ** is exponentiation; ^ is integer bitwise exclusive OR.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Python integers is accurate?
choices: Precision grows subject to available memory
questions.explanation: Python integers do not have a fixed-width overflow boundary.

questions.prompt: What does input() return when a user types digits?
questions.explanation: input reads text; numeric conversion and validation must be explicit.

questions.prompt: Which built-in function reveals an object's type?
questions.explanation: type returns the object's class; the other functions answer different questions.

questions.prompt: Which condition safely requires a non-None positive value?
choices: value is not None and value > 0
value is not None or value > 0
questions.explanation: and skips the numeric comparison when the value is None.

questions.prompt: Why is id() unsuitable as a persistent record identifier across runs?
choices: id is a permanent database key
Equal values always have the same id forever
Identity is a runtime property tied to an object's lifetime
questions.explanation: Use a stable business or generated identifier for persisted records.

questions.prompt: What substring does this half-open slice produce?
questions.code: print('dataEngineering'[1:4])
questions.explanation: The stop is excluded, so positions 1, 2 and 3 are selected.

questions.prompt: What does the negative string index select?
questions.code: print('spark'[-1])
questions.explanation: Index -1 selects the final character.

questions.prompt: What does the reverse string slice print?
questions.code: print('data'[::-1])
questions.explanation: A step of -1 traverses the sequence backward.

questions.prompt: What does a slice beyond the string's end print?
questions.code: print('spark'[1:99])
questions.explanation: Slice bounds are clipped to the sequence length.

questions.prompt: Which exception does string item assignment raise?
questions.code:
name = 'etl'
name[0] = 'E'
print(name)
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable and do not support item assignment.

questions.prompt: What remains after upper() is called without saving its result?
questions.code:
name = 'etl'
name.upper()
print(name)
questions.explanation: upper returns a new string and leaves the original unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does default whitespace splitting produce?
questions.code: print(' a  b '.split())
questions.explanation: split() collapses whitespace runs and discards empty edge fields.

questions.prompt: What does splitting on an explicit space preserve?
questions.code: print('a  b'.split(' '))
questions.explanation: Adjacent explicit separators create empty fields.

questions.prompt: What text does join produce here?
questions.code: print('/'.join(['raw', 'clean', 'gold']))
questions.explanation: join inserts its separator between strings, not at their edges.

questions.prompt: What does character-set stripping produce?
questions.code: print('abcab'.strip('ab'))
questions.explanation: strip('ab') removes any a or b repeatedly from both ends.

questions.prompt: What does a replacement count of one produce?
questions.code: print('a-b-a'.replace('a', 'x', 1))
questions.explanation: The count limits replacements, starting from the left.

questions.prompt: What does find print when the substring is absent?
questions.code: print('batch'.find('z'))
questions.explanation: find returns -1 for absence; index raises ValueError instead.

questions.prompt: What does count print for these overlapping-looking matches?
questions.code: print('aaaa'.count('aa'))
questions.explanation: count counts non-overlapping occurrences.

questions.prompt: What formatted value does the f-string print?
questions.explanation: .2f formats two digits after the decimal point.

questions.prompt: What does partition return when its separator is absent?
questions.code: print('key'.partition('='))
questions.explanation: partition always produces three parts; the original occupies the first when no separator exists.

questions.prompt: What does this Unicode caseless comparison print?
questions.code: print('Straße'.casefold() == 'STRASSE'.casefold())
questions.explanation: casefold includes mappings such as German sharp s to ss.

questions.prompt: Which method removes one exact prefix if present?
questions.explanation: removeprefix treats its argument as a complete prefix, not a set of characters.

questions.prompt: Which operation converts text to UTF-8 bytes?
questions.explanation: Encoding maps text to bytes; decoding reverses the process.

questions.prompt: Which operation interprets UTF-8 bytes as text?
questions.explanation: decode interprets the encoding; str(bytes) normally shows a bytes representation.

questions.prompt: Why can len(text) differ from the number of visible symbols?
choices: len rounds to powers of two
Some symbols span multiple Unicode code points
questions.explanation: Strings count code points, while combining marks and emoji can form multi-code-point symbols.

questions.prompt: Which expression checks for a '.csv' filename suffix?
questions.explanation: endswith checks a complete suffix; one index retrieves one character.

questions.prompt: How should a list of integers be joined with commas?
choices: Convert each integer to str before joining
Convert the whole list to int
questions.explanation: join requires string elements, for example ','.join(map(str, numbers)).

questions.prompt: Before lowercasing a data key, what should an engineer establish?
choices: The key's normalization and case-sensitivity rules
questions.explanation: Case conversion can merge distinct case-sensitive business keys.

questions.prompt: Which method checks for a nonempty string of Unicode decimal characters?
questions.explanation: isdecimal includes Unicode decimal characters beyond ASCII digits.

questions.prompt: Why does isdigit() alone reject a valid signed integer string?
choices: It raises on every empty string
A leading sign is not a digit
questions.explanation: A '-' character makes isdigit false even if int can parse the text.

questions.prompt: Which syntax supports a multiline string literal?
questions.explanation: Triple-quoted literals may include literal newline characters.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a raw string such as r'\d+'?
choices: Avoid most Python backslash escape processing
questions.explanation: A raw string preserves backslashes conveniently; another library can still interpret them.

questions.prompt: Which operation splits at only the final occurrence of a delimiter?
questions.explanation: rsplit starts from the right; a one-split limit preserves earlier delimiters.

questions.prompt: Which expression checks for 'error' anywhere in a message?
questions.explanation: Substring membership accepts a match anywhere in the string.

questions.prompt: Why can repeated concatenation of many strings be inefficient?
choices: It may repeatedly allocate and copy an expanding result
Strings are stored only on disk
questions.explanation: Collecting pieces and joining them avoids repeated rebuilding in typical implementations.

questions.prompt: What does appending through a list alias print?
questions.code:
a = [1]
b = a
b.append(2)
print(a)
questions.explanation: Both names refer to the same mutable list.

questions.code:
a = [1]
b = a.copy()
b.append(2)
print(a)
questions.explanation: copy creates a distinct outer list, so appending to b does not change a.

questions.code:

b = a.copy()
b[0].append(2)
print(a)
questions.explanation: The outer lists differ but share the same inner list.

questions.prompt: What does append do with a list argument?
questions.code:
values = [1]

print(values)

questions.code:

values.extend([2, 3])
print(values)
questions.explanation: extend consumes the iterable and adds its elements.

questions.code:
values = [3, 1, 2]
result = values.sort()
print(result)
questions.explanation: sort changes the existing list and returns None.

questions.prompt: What does sorted leave in its original input?
questions.code:
values = [3, 1, 2]
sorted(values)
print(values)
questions.explanation: sorted returns a new list without mutating the input.

questions.prompt: What does list.pop() return without an index?
questions.code:
values = [10, 20, 30]
print(values.pop())
questions.explanation: pop removes and returns the final element by default.

questions.prompt: What remains after list.remove finds the first match?
questions.code:
values = [1, 2, 1]
values.remove(1)
print(values)
questions.explanation: remove deletes the first equal value, not every occurrence.

questions.prompt: What does multiplying a nested list repeat?
questions.code:

rows[0][0] = 9
print(rows)
questions.explanation: Repetition repeats references to one inner list.

questions.prompt: What does starred sequence unpacking collect?
questions.code:

print(middle)
questions.explanation: A starred target receives a list of the remaining intervening elements.

questions.explanation: The trailing comma creates a one-element tuple.

record[0].append(2)
print(record)
questions.explanation: The tuple keeps the same reference while its contained list changes.

questions.prompt: What does this slice assignment produce?
questions.code:

values[1:3] = [8, 9]
print(values)
questions.explanation: Slice assignment replaces the selected region with the provided elements.

questions.prompt: What does ordinary list addition leave in an old alias?

b = a

print(b)

questions.code:

b = a
a += [2]
print(b)
questions.explanation: List += extends the existing list, so aliases observe it.

questions.prompt: Which expression inserts an item at the list's beginning?

choices: When all its elements are hashable
questions.explanation: Tuple hashability depends on its elements.

questions.prompt: What happens when three elements are unpacked into exactly two names?

choices: Index shifts can cause items to be skipped
Lists are immutable during every loop

The entire list length regardless of x

When nested mutable values must become independent too
Whenever a list exceeds ten items

questions.prompt: Why can a tuple communicate intent for a coordinate pair?
choices: It guarantees smaller memory use in every implementation

questions.prompt: What does a virtual environment primarily isolate?

choices: Convert nested Row values into nested dictionaries too
Sort every dictionary key by value
questions.explanation: The recursive option converts nested Row structures. It does not execute a DataFrame action on its own.

questions.prompt: What does nullable=True on a StructField permit?
choices: A null value for that field
Only null values for that field
Automatic replacement of null with zero
questions.explanation: Nullability allows absence; the data type still constrains non-null values.

questions.prompt: An ArrayType(StringType(), containsNull=False) field itself is nullable=True. Which value is consistent with that contract?
choices: Every array must contain at least one null
The whole array can never be null
Null elements are permitted whenever the outer field is nullable
The whole array may be null, but an existing array cannot contain null elements
questions.explanation: Field nullability and element nullability are separate schema properties.

questions.prompt: What restriction applies to keys in a Spark MapType?
choices: Map keys must be consecutive integers
Map keys must have unique column names
All map keys must be strings
questions.explanation: MapType forbids null keys. Its valueContainsNull setting controls null values instead.

questions.prompt: Which schema represents an array of integer values?
questions.explanation: ArrayType takes the element type; MapType additionally requires key and value types.

questions.prompt: Given a Python integer with ordinary schema inference, which Spark type is commonly inferred?
choices: ByteType based on the first small value
questions.explanation: Python integers are inferred as Spark long values in ordinary local-data inference, rather than choosing the narrowest integer type.

questions.prompt: Why can inferring a column containing only None fail?
choices: None is illegal in every DataFrame
Spark converts None into a table name
Every null column is automatically a BooleanType
There is no non-null value establishing its concrete type
questions.explanation: An explicit schema resolves ambiguity for columns with no typed values.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of cast("int") on a Column?
choices: Convert the DataFrame to a Python iterator
Request conversion of values to an integer type
questions.explanation: cast changes the expression's target type. Invalid conversions depend on SQL mode and input.

questions.prompt: What is the selected value for this valid numeric conversion?
questions.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
spark.range(1).select(F.lit("42").cast("int").alias("n"))
questions.explanation: The string contains a valid integer representation, so casting produces the integer 42.

questions.prompt: What do the names supplied in this creation specify?
questions.code: spark.createDataFrame([(1, "x")], ["id", "label"])
choices: Column names while Spark infers types from the data
The values of the first row
The partitioning keys of the output
questions.explanation: A list of names labels inferred columns; it does not itself declare their types.

questions.prompt: Which Python value naturally corresponds to Spark BinaryType?
questions.explanation: BinaryType represents byte sequences. Application or file-handle objects are not binary column values.

questions.prompt: Which Python object is appropriate for an explicitly declared DecimalType field?
choices: A string plus a scale argument on the Row
float("12.50") as an exact decimal guarantee
questions.explanation: Decimal values preserve base-ten representation and match an explicit DecimalType contract.

questions.prompt: What does df.dtypes return?
choices: All row values converted to Python types
Pairs of column names and type strings
A list of driver process IDs
questions.explanation: dtypes describes each column as a name/type pair without returning the dataset's rows.

questions.prompt: What change does this operation perform?
questions.code: renamed = df.toDF("customer_id", "city")
choices: It renames the two columns without declaring new types
It casts every value to string
It turns the rows into a dictionary
questions.explanation: toDF with names changes the column names. Types are retained from the source DataFrame.

questions.prompt: Why should a test compare nested schemas as well as visible row values?
choices: Two matching samples guarantee every schema is identical
Nested schemas are ignored by Spark
Schema comparisons replace all value assertions
Nested field types and nullability affect downstream contracts even when sample values look alike
questions.explanation: Rows alone may not reveal differences such as integer versus string elements or nested nullability.

questions.prompt: Which field type models an object with named subfields such as street and postcode?
questions.explanation: A struct provides named, typed nested fields, unlike an array's ordered homogeneous elements.

questions.prompt: What will this schema inspection identify for amount?
questions.code:
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, DecimalType
schema = StructType([StructField("amount", DecimalType(8, 2))])
choices: A string limited to eight characters
A decimal field with precision 8 and scale 2
An array with eight two-element entries
A binary float rounded only for display
questions.explanation: The schema declares exact decimal precision and scale rather than a display format.

questions.prompt: Why is explicit schema review important before unioning independently ingested datasets?
choices: The same-looking columns may have different types or positions
Union always matches fields by business meaning
All files force identical field types
Spark silently validates every business rule during inference
questions.explanation: Schema differences can cause coercion, errors or incorrect alignment. Make the contract explicit before combining data.

questions.prompt: What does F.col("price") represent?
choices: A collected Python list of prices
The literal string price in every row
A column expression referring to price
questions.explanation: col builds a reference that Spark resolves against a DataFrame plan.

questions.prompt: Which function creates a constant column expression?
questions.explanation: lit wraps a literal value so it can participate in Column expressions.

questions.prompt: What does select primarily control?
choices: How long the test runner waits
Which expressions appear as output columns
questions.explanation: select is a projection: it chooses or calculates output fields.

questions.prompt: What happens when withColumn uses an existing column name?
choices: That column is replaced in the returned DataFrame
The original DataFrame is changed in place
Spark always creates two identically named fields
questions.explanation: withColumn returns a new DataFrame with the specified column added or replaced.

questions.prompt: For an input row amount=10, what is net in this result?
questions.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
out = df.select((F.col("amount") - 2).alias("net"))
questions.explanation: The Column subtraction is evaluated for the row, producing 10 minus 2.

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly combines two PySpark column comparisons with AND?
questions.explanation: Use parenthesized bitwise operators overloaded by Column. Python boolean operators attempt driver-side truth conversion.

questions.prompt: Why does this predicate raise an error instead of filtering rows?
questions.code: df.filter((df.x > 0) and (df.y < 5))
choices: Both comparisons must use a UDF
Python and tries to convert a Column to a single boolean
questions.explanation: Columns represent row-wise expressions and cannot be used as a single Python truth value.

questions.prompt: Which operation renames an expression in a select result?
questions.explanation: Column.alias sets an output name for the expression.

questions.prompt: Given amount=25, what value does this expression produce?
questions.code: F.when(F.col("amount") >= 20, "large").otherwise("small")
questions.explanation: The condition is true, so when selects the first branch.

questions.prompt: Given amount=5, what does the following expression return?
questions.code: F.when(F.col("amount") > 10, "high")
questions.explanation: Without otherwise, rows matching no when condition receive null.

questions.prompt: Which is an alias of DataFrame.filter?
questions.explanation: where and filter express the same row-filtering operation.

questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between F.col("active") and F.lit("active")?
choices: The first references a field; the second repeats a string constant
The first collects rows while the second sorts
questions.explanation: The distinction between references and constants prevents many expression bugs.

questions.prompt: With columns x=2 and y=3, what does this projection produce?
questions.code: df.selectExpr("x + y AS total")
choices: Two fields named x and y only
questions.explanation: selectExpr parses SQL expressions and their aliases into a DataFrame projection.

questions.prompt: Which expression negates a boolean Column predicate?
questions.explanation: The overloaded ~ operator creates a Spark NOT expression. Python not does not operate row by row.

questions.prompt: Why are parentheses important around comparisons joined by &?
choices: Parentheses turn Columns into Python booleans
Python operator precedence can otherwise construct the wrong expression
Parentheses force a separate Spark job per row
questions.explanation: Explicit parentheses ensure comparisons are formed before their boolean combination.

questions.prompt: Which rows satisfy this filter when status is non-null?
questions.code: df.filter(F.col("status").isin("new", "retry"))
choices: Rows whose status is either new or retry
Rows whose status contains both words
Rows whose status is any non-empty string
Only rows whose status is null
questions.explanation: isin checks membership in the specified values.

questions.prompt: What does between(10, 20) mean for non-null numeric values?
questions.explanation: between includes both boundary values.

questions.prompt: Which call removes named columns from a returned DataFrame?
questions.explanation: drop removes columns; filter selects rows using a condition.

questions.prompt: What happens to df after assigning df2 here?
questions.code: df2 = df.select("id")
choices: df's rows are collected into df2
df still represents its original columns
df is permanently reduced to id
questions.explanation: DataFrame transformations return new plans rather than mutating the original variable's object.

questions.prompt: Which expression selects a top-level column whose literal name contains a dot?
questions.explanation: Backticks distinguish a literal dotted field name from nested-field access syntax.

questions.prompt: Why might df["count"] be clearer than df.count when referencing a column named count?
choices: Bracket access forces all rows into memory
Attribute access always casts columns to strings
Attribute lookup can resolve to the DataFrame method rather than the column
questions.explanation: Bracket or explicit col references avoid collisions with DataFrame attributes and methods.

questions.prompt: What does F.expr accept?
choices: Only a list of Row objects
questions.explanation: expr parses SQL expression syntax into a Column usable in the DataFrame API.

questions.prompt: Which result does this expression produce for x=4?
questions.code: df.select(F.expr("x * x").alias("square"))
questions.explanation: expr parses the multiplication as a Spark SQL expression.

questions.prompt: What does df.select("*") request?
choices: All rows copied into the driver
questions.explanation: The star expands to the DataFrame's columns. It remains a DataFrame projection.

questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation of df.limit(10)?
choices: A Python list in input insertion order
A DataFrame containing at most ten rows, with no guaranteed choice absent ordering
questions.explanation: limit caps row count. A deterministic top-ten result needs an explicit ordering rule.

questions.prompt: How should you obtain the ten greatest non-null scores deterministically when scores can tie and id is unique?
choices: Use collect and trust partition order
Use distinct on score and ignore id
Order by score descending and id as a tie-breaker, then limit ten
Call limit ten before ordering by score
questions.explanation: A total ordering plus limit defines a reproducible top set, including boundary ties.

questions.prompt: Which expression turns a nullable status into a two-category label with an explicit fallback?
questions.explanation: The otherwise branch handles rows where the condition is false or unknown, including null status.

questions.prompt: What does this selected constant do for a three-row input?
questions.code: df.select("id", F.lit("batch").alias("source"))
choices: Adds the value batch to each of the three output rows
Filters out rows without an existing batch field
questions.explanation: lit produces the constant for each input row; alias names the output field.

questions.prompt: Why should a transformation function usually return the DataFrame it constructs?
choices: Spark automatically replaces every caller variable
Python cannot pass DataFrames as arguments
The caller needs the new plan because transformations do not mutate the input
questions.explanation: Returning the transformed DataFrame makes composition explicit and avoids accidentally retaining the original plan.

questions.prompt: A filter condition evaluates to SQL NULL for a row. Does that row pass?
choices: Yes; all unknown rows pass by default
It always crashes the Spark application
No; filter retains only rows with a true predicate
Yes; NULL is treated as true
questions.explanation: SQL filtering excludes false and unknown predicates. Use explicit null handling when null rows should remain.

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly detects a SQL null in column city?
questions.explanation: isNull builds the intended Spark predicate. The string NULL is ordinary text, and Python identity is not row-wise evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which expression keeps rows where id is present?
questions.explanation: isNotNull tests values in the column. Testing a literal string would be true for every row.

questions.prompt: What is the SQL result of NULL = NULL?
questions.explanation: Ordinary equality cannot establish equality of unknown values. Null-safe equality is a different operator.

questions.prompt: What is the SQL result of NULL <=> NULL?
choices: A syntax error in Spark SQL
questions.explanation: The null-safe equality operator treats two nulls as equal.

questions.prompt: What does this expression produce for a=null and b=null?
questions.code: F.col("a").eqNullSafe(F.col("b"))
questions.explanation: eqNullSafe implements null-safe equality, including equality of two null operands.

questions.prompt: Which rows remain after this filter for x values 1, -1 and null?
questions.code: df.filter(F.col("x") > 0)
questions.explanation: The null comparison is unknown, and filter retains only true predicates.

questions.prompt: Which predicate keeps positive x values as well as missing x values?
questions.explanation: An OR explicitly includes missing values. Combining positive and null tests with AND cannot match the same value.

questions.prompt: Which function returns the first non-null argument?
questions.explanation: coalesce evaluates expressions in order and chooses the first available value.

questions.prompt: What is the result here for primary=null and backup="west"?
questions.code: F.coalesce(F.col("primary"), F.col("backup"), F.lit("unknown"))
questions.explanation: The second expression is the first non-null value, so the final fallback is unused.

questions.prompt: Does SQL NULL mean the same thing as an empty string?
choices: No; an empty string is a present string value
No, because empty strings are always invalid
questions.explanation: A missing value and a zero-length string require different validation rules.

questions.prompt: Which function detects floating-point NaN values?
questions.explanation: isnan checks the special floating-point NaN value. NaN is not SQL null.

questions.prompt: For a floating-point NaN value, what does isNull() return?
choices: It converts NaN to zero first
questions.explanation: Spark distinguishes NaN from missing values, so a null test alone does not identify NaN.

questions.prompt: How does Spark SQL equality treat NaN compared with NaN?
choices: As unequal like ordinary Python float equality
questions.explanation: Spark SQL gives NaN special semantics, including NaN equality. Do not assume Python floating-point equality rules apply unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which call removes rows containing null or NaN in any considered column by default?
questions.explanation: na.drop removes rows according to missing-value criteria. drop with a string removes a column instead.

questions.prompt: What does this cleaning rule require to retain a row?
questions.code: df.na.drop(thresh=2, subset=["a", "b", "c"])
choices: Two distinct values anywhere in the dataset
At least two non-null/non-NaN values among a, b and c
questions.explanation: thresh specifies a minimum number of present values in the considered columns.

questions.prompt: What rows are removed by this rule?
questions.code: df.na.drop(how="all", subset=["a", "b"])
choices: Rows with any missing field anywhere
Rows where a and b are equal
Rows where both a and b are missing
Rows where either a or b is missing
questions.explanation: how='all' drops a row only when all considered values are missing.

questions.prompt: Why specify subset when dropping rows with missing required identifiers?
choices: To change every nullable schema flag
To avoid discarding rows only because optional fields are missing
To fill missing identifiers with a subset name
questions.explanation: A targeted subset encodes which fields are required rather than imposing completeness on every column.

questions.prompt: Which call fills missing numeric amount values with zero?
questions.explanation: A fill dictionary maps column names to replacement values.

questions.prompt: What does filling string columns with "unknown" do to a null integer column?
choices: It is always converted to the string unknown
It is not filled by that incompatible string replacement
questions.explanation: fillna applies replacements to compatible column types, so a generic string fill is not a universal missing-value rule.

questions.prompt: What value results for s="   " from this normalization?
questions.code: F.when(F.trim(F.col("s")) == "", F.lit(None)).otherwise(F.col("s"))
questions.explanation: Trimming yields the empty string, which the explicit when branch converts to null.

questions.prompt: What does DataFrame.distinct compare when removing duplicates?
choices: All selected columns of each row
questions.explanation: distinct deduplicates complete rows in the current projection.

questions.prompt: Given rows (1,"A") and (1,"B"), what is guaranteed by dropDuplicates(["id"])?
choices: One row for id=1, with no guaranteed choice of payload
The row with payload B always survives
The row with payload A always survives
Both rows survive because payloads differ
questions.explanation: Subset deduplication uses the key but does not define a deterministic winner among differing payloads.

questions.prompt: Which strategy reliably selects the latest record per key when timestamps can tie?
choices: dropDuplicates on the key after an unrelated display sort
row_number over a key-partitioned window ordered by timestamp and a unique tie-breaker
questions.explanation: A complete ordered selection rule defines which record wins, including ties.

questions.prompt: How are null grouping keys treated by groupBy?
choices: Grouping by nullable columns is forbidden
Every null row receives its own random group
questions.explanation: Grouping treats null keys as belonging to the same group, unlike ordinary equality predicates.

questions.prompt: What is the result of TRUE OR NULL in Spark SQL?
questions.explanation: A true operand makes OR true even when the other operand is unknown.

questions.prompt: What is the result of FALSE AND NULL in Spark SQL?
questions.explanation: A false operand makes AND false; the unknown operand cannot make the conjunction true.

questions.prompt: What does NOT NULL evaluate to in SQL boolean logic?
questions.explanation: Negating an unknown truth value still yields unknown.

questions.prompt: For x values 2, null and 5, what does this aggregation produce?
questions.code: df.agg(F.count("x").alias("n"))
questions.explanation: count(column) excludes nulls. count(*) would count all three rows.

questions.prompt: Why can NOT IN behave unexpectedly when the comparison list contains NULL?
choices: Spark rewrites NULL to zero automatically
For unmatched values, the predicate can be unknown rather than true
NULL forces every input value to match
NOT IN ignores all non-null list values
questions.explanation: SQL three-valued logic affects membership tests. Model missing values explicitly when constructing exclusion rules.

questions.prompt: What is a sound validation step before replacing all missing monetary values with zero?
choices: Confirm that missing means zero rather than unknown or failed ingestion
Assume every numeric null is zero by definition
Replace the entire schema with strings
Drop the source identifier so errors cannot be traced
questions.explanation: A technically valid fill can change business meaning. Cleaning rules should follow a documented data contract.

questions.prompt: Which function removes leading and trailing spaces from a string column?
questions.explanation: trim removes surrounding spaces; it does not remove arbitrary internal whitespace.

questions.prompt: For s="  Ada  ", what does this expression return?
questions.code: F.lower(F.trim(F.col("s")))
questions.explanation: trim removes the outer spaces and lower normalizes the letters to lowercase.

questions.prompt: Which function replaces text matching a regular expression?
questions.explanation: regexp_replace applies a pattern-based replacement inside string values.

questions.prompt: For s="A-12-B", what is the result?
questions.code: F.regexp_replace(F.col("s"), "[0-9]+", "")
questions.explanation: The pattern matches the consecutive digits, replacing them with an empty string.

questions.prompt: What is produced for s="east|west"?
questions.code: F.split(F.col("s"), "[|]")
choices: A map from east to west
An array containing east and west
questions.explanation: split returns an array. The vertical bar must be treated literally in the regular expression.

questions.prompt: In Spark SQL substring, what is the starting index for the first character?
questions.explanation: substring uses SQL-style one-based positions rather than Python's zero-based indexing.

questions.prompt: What is the result for s="abcdef"?
questions.code: F.substring(F.col("s"), 2, 3)
questions.explanation: A starting position of 2 means b, and a length of 3 selects bcd.

questions.prompt: How does concat_ws("-", "a", "b") handle a null value in b when a="x"?
choices: It returns x, skipping the null string input
questions.explanation: concat_ws skips null string inputs. This differs from assuming every concatenation propagates null.

questions.prompt: Which function measures the length of a string value?
questions.explanation: length measures string length; count is an aggregation over rows or values.

questions.prompt: Which predicate tests whether a string column starts with "INV-"?
questions.explanation: startswith performs a prefix test. Equality does not interpret percent as a wildcard.

questions.prompt: Which predicate uses SQL LIKE wildcards to find codes beginning with AB?
questions.explanation: In SQL LIKE, percent matches any-length text. An asterisk is not the corresponding wildcard.

questions.prompt: What does regexp_extract return when its pattern has no match in a non-null string?
choices: A Python exception for every row
questions.explanation: regexp_extract returns an empty string when the regex or requested group does not match; null input is a separate case.

questions.prompt: Which function parses a string into DateType using an optional format?
questions.explanation: to_date converts input into a date. date_format creates formatted text from a temporal value.

questions.prompt: What type is produced by this expression?
questions.code: F.to_date(F.col("day_text"), "yyyy-MM-dd")
questions.explanation: to_date returns a calendar-date value, not merely a reformatted string.

questions.prompt: What type is produced by this expression?
questions.code: F.date_format(F.col("event_date"), "yyyy/MM/dd")
questions.explanation: date_format formats a date or timestamp as text. Keep this distinction when designing downstream schemas.

questions.prompt: Which call adds seven calendar days to a date column?
questions.explanation: date_add advances by a number of days. add_months advances by calendar months.

questions.prompt: What is returned by this calculation?
questions.explanation: datediff returns end minus start in calendar days, so January 3 minus January 1 is two.

questions.prompt: What date is produced here?
questions.code: F.add_months(F.to_date(F.lit("2024-01-31")), 1)
questions.explanation: add_months adjusts to the last valid day when the target month is shorter; 2024 is a leap year.

questions.prompt: Which function returns the final calendar date of the input month?
questions.explanation: last_day computes month-end; dayofmonth extracts an integer day number.

questions.prompt: Which value does this expression produce?
questions.code: F.month(F.to_date(F.lit("2024-02-29")))
questions.explanation: month extracts the month number from a date, so February is 2.

questions.prompt: What does dayofweek return for a Sunday in Spark SQL?
questions.explanation: Spark's dayofweek numbering starts with Sunday as 1. Do not substitute ISO weekday numbering without checking the function.

questions.prompt: Why should timestamps without offsets have a documented source time zone?
choices: A source time zone changes only the column name
Time zones never affect timestamp parsing
Their intended instant can change depending on how local clock time is interpreted
All unzoned timestamps are necessarily UTC
questions.explanation: Local wall-clock text is ambiguous without a zone policy, especially near daylight-saving transitions.

questions.prompt: Which setting commonly controls session-level timestamp parsing and display interpretation?
questions.explanation: The session time zone affects temporal interpretation and rendering; resource settings do not define time zones.

questions.prompt: A field is already a DateType and is needed for date arithmetic. What is the best default approach?
choices: Keep it as DateType and use date functions
Format it as dd/MM/yyyy and do lexical arithmetic
Convert every date to a Python string on the driver
Treat month numbers as elapsed days
questions.explanation: Typed dates preserve calendar semantics and avoid text-order mistakes.

questions.prompt: Which expression extracts the first capturing group of digits from code="INV-104"?
questions.explanation: Group 1 refers to the parenthesized digits. Group 0 represents the whole regex match.

questions.prompt: For a date column d, which function returns an integer year?
questions.explanation: year returns the numeric year; date_format produces text and trunc produces a date boundary.

questions.prompt: What is the calendar date returned here?
questions.code: F.trunc(F.to_date(F.lit("2024-05-17")), "month")
questions.explanation: trunc with month returns the first date of the input month.

questions.prompt: Why can calling a Python datetime parser directly on F.col("raw_time") fail conceptually?
choices: The argument is a symbolic Column, not an individual Python string
Spark columns always contain only integers
datetime parsing is impossible in Spark
Every Column is already a timezone-aware datetime
questions.explanation: Use Spark expressions or a properly declared UDF; Python scalar functions do not automatically operate over symbolic Columns.

questions.prompt: What is a sound test set for a timestamp parsing rule?
choices: Only values after converting all timestamps to arbitrary strings
Valid values, nulls, malformed text, offsets and relevant clock-change boundaries
questions.explanation: Parsing rules need boundary and failure cases, not just a single happy-path example.

questions.prompt: Which statement about current_timestamp within one query is correct?
choices: It always returns the Unix epoch
It returns the operating system timezone name
Calls in the same query use the same query-start timestamp value
Every row necessarily gets a different time
questions.explanation: Spark evaluates current_timestamp consistently at query start for that query, rather than as a separate wall-clock call per row.

questions.prompt: What does groupBy("customer") establish?
choices: The key defining each aggregation group
The permanent physical order of all rows
A mandatory unique constraint on customer
questions.explanation: groupBy specifies grouping keys; agg or another aggregation then computes measures for them.

questions.prompt: Which expression counts all rows in a group, including rows with null amount?
questions.explanation: count(*) counts rows independently of a particular nullable measure.

questions.prompt: For amount values 10, null and 20, what is count(amount)?
questions.explanation: count of a column ignores null values, leaving two present amounts.

questions.prompt: For amount values 10, null and 20, what is avg(amount)?
questions.explanation: Average divides the sum of non-null values by their count, so 30 divided by 2 is 15.

questions.prompt: For a group whose amount values are all null, what does sum(amount) return?
questions.explanation: sum has no non-null values to accumulate and returns null. Use an explicit fallback only when business meaning supports it.

questions.prompt: Which operation calculates a summary for the entire DataFrame without named group keys?
questions.explanation: agg on a DataFrame is a global aggregation, returning the overall measure.

questions.prompt: What is the output grain of this query?
questions.code: orders.groupBy("customer", "day").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
choices: One row for the entire dataset
One row per distinct customer and day pair
questions.explanation: Both fields participate in the grouping key.

questions.prompt: Given rows (A,2), (A,3), (B,4), what total is produced for A?
questions.code: df.groupBy("key").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
questions.explanation: The two amounts associated with A are summed; B belongs to another group.

questions.prompt: Which syntax calculates two named measures in one grouped aggregation?
questions.explanation: GroupedData.agg accepts multiple aggregate expressions, each with a useful output alias.

questions.prompt: Which function counts distinct non-null values of a single column exactly?
questions.explanation: countDistinct removes duplicate values for the count and excludes null values in a single-column distinct count.

questions.prompt: For x values 1, 1, 2 and null, what does countDistinct(x) return?
questions.explanation: The distinct present values are 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate preserves repeated values when building an array?
questions.explanation: collect_list retains duplicates. Its distributed output order is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: What is guaranteed about collect_set on non-null input values A, A and B?
choices: It contains A and B once each, without a guaranteed element order
It contains A, A and B in input order
It always returns the string AB
questions.explanation: collect_set removes duplicate elements, but array ordering should not be assumed.

questions.prompt: Why is first("status") after an unordered groupBy unsuitable for selecting the newest status?
choices: It does not define which event is newest or guarantee the chosen row
first always sorts by event time automatically
first always returns the lexicographically greatest status
questions.explanation: Selecting the newest record requires an ordering rule, usually expressed with a window or a suitable ordered aggregate.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of ignorenulls=True in F.first("x", ignorenulls=True)?
choices: Fill all null values with the first row
Skip null values when choosing a first value within the aggregation's encountered order
questions.explanation: Ignoring nulls changes value eligibility; it does not create a deterministic event-time order.

questions.prompt: What does pivot do to category values?
choices: Always transposes the full table exactly like a local matrix
Turns selected category values into output columns
Turns every column into an executor
questions.explanation: Pivot combines grouping and aggregation to create columns from category values.

questions.prompt: Why supply an explicit list of pivot values when the categories are known?
choices: It forces one output row per input row
It defines intended output categories and avoids discovering all distinct pivot values first
It makes nulls equal to zero automatically
questions.explanation: An explicit pivot list controls the columns and avoids a distinct-value discovery step.

questions.prompt: What columns, besides store, are targeted by this pivot?
questions.code: sales.groupBy("store").pivot("channel", ["web", "shop"]).sum("amount")
choices: One column for every amount value
questions.explanation: The supplied pivot values become category columns with aggregated amounts.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes rollup(a, b) from a plain groupBy(a, b)?
choices: rollup includes hierarchical subtotals and a grand total
questions.explanation: Rollup adds subtotal grouping levels following the specified hierarchy.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes cube(a, b) from rollup(a, b)?
choices: cube returns only the grand total
cube is an alias for distinct
cube includes every combination of the grouping dimensions
cube always uses exactly three dimensions
questions.explanation: Cube requests all grouping combinations; rollup requests a hierarchy of prefixes.

questions.prompt: Why can grouping() be useful with rollup results containing null keys?
choices: It converts null into an empty array
It distinguishes a subtotal-generated null from a null present in source data
It replaces every null with a row number
questions.explanation: Grouping indicators identify whether a dimension was aggregated away at a subtotal level.

questions.prompt: Which aggregation counts only rows with status="failed"?
questions.explanation: Summing indicator values counts matches. Counting a non-null boolean counts false values too.

questions.prompt: Why is count(col("status") == "failed") usually not the desired failure count?
choices: count counts non-null boolean results, including false
questions.explanation: count(expression) counts present results rather than only true results.

questions.prompt: What is this code's return type before a subsequent action?
questions.code: summary = df.agg(F.min("x").alias("lo"), F.max("x").alias("hi"))
choices: A GroupedData object with no aggregation
questions.explanation: agg produces a DataFrame containing the aggregate results; collect or another action can retrieve them.

questions.prompt: Which result is produced for the global count over an empty DataFrame?
choices: A missing-table error solely because it is empty
A single result row with count 0
A result row with count NULL
questions.explanation: A global count returns zero for an empty input. Grouped aggregation with no groups has different output cardinality.

questions.prompt: Which function estimates distinct cardinality when approximation is acceptable?
questions.explanation: approx_count_distinct trades exactness for an approximate cardinality computation.

questions.prompt: Why must averaging per-partition averages account for each partition's number of non-null values?
choices: All partition averages are inherently equal
The global average is always the sum of partition averages
Unequal counts require a weighted combination to recover the overall average
questions.explanation: An unweighted average of averages is generally wrong when group sizes differ; combine sums and counts.

questions.prompt: Which measure answers how many different customer-product pairs occurred?
questions.explanation: A multi-column distinct count counts distinct combinations, subject to its null handling, rather than summing separate counts.

questions.prompt: How can you make a collected list of non-null integers sorted after grouping?
choices: Use countDistinct instead of an array
questions.explanation: Sorting the resulting array imposes element order; distributed encounter order is not reliable.

questions.prompt: What mistake does this query illustrate if amount is not a grouping field?
questions.code: SELECT customer, amount, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer
choices: Selecting a raw amount beside a grouped aggregate lacks a rule for choosing one amount
Every sum requires a Python loop
Grouping can only use numeric keys
A count must always accompany sum
questions.explanation: A grouped result needs each output to be a grouping expression or a valid aggregate expression.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps only matching row pairs from both inputs?
questions.explanation: An inner join returns pairs satisfying the join condition, excluding unmatched rows.

questions.prompt: Which join preserves every left row even when no right row matches?
questions.explanation: A left outer join emits unmatched left rows with null values for right-side fields.

questions.prompt: Which join returns left rows that have at least one right match without adding right columns?
questions.explanation: A left semi join tests existence and returns only the left schema.

questions.prompt: Which join is suited to finding fact rows whose key has no matching dimension row?
questions.explanation: A left anti join keeps left rows with no match under the specified condition.

questions.prompt: A key appears twice on the left and three times on the right. How many pairs does an inner equijoin produce for that key?
questions.explanation: Each matching left row pairs with each matching right row: 2 multiplied by 3.

questions.prompt: Why can adding a dimension join unexpectedly increase a fact table's row count?
choices: Spark adds one audit row per executor
Every join inserts all missing keys
The dimension may contain multiple matches for a fact key
Inner joins always preserve the left row count
questions.explanation: Duplicate right-side keys multiply matched fact rows. Check the expected relationship cardinality.

questions.prompt: What schema behavior is expected for the shared id key here?
questions.code: left.join(right, ["id"], "inner")
choices: The id column becomes an array
The result has one id join-key column
The result always has two id columns
The id column is removed entirely
questions.explanation: Joining by common column names treats those keys as a single output key column.

questions.prompt: How does an explicit equality join differ regarding the two original key columns?
questions.code: left.alias("l").join(right.alias("r"), F.col("l.id") == F.col("r.id"))
choices: Both key columns can remain, requiring qualified selection
Both key columns are always removed
The right key is always renamed automatically
The left key is always converted to a string
questions.explanation: An expression join may preserve both input fields, so aliases and explicit projection avoid ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Do null keys match each other under ordinary equality in an inner join?
choices: Yes, every null key matches every null key
Only if the left input is larger
Only when the key is a string
No, because the equality condition is unknown
questions.explanation: Ordinary null equality does not yield true. Use null-safe equality only when that matches the intended relationship.

questions.prompt: Which join condition deliberately matches two null key values?
questions.explanation: eqNullSafe makes the desired null-equality behavior explicit.

questions.prompt: What does a cross join return for nonempty inputs?
choices: One row per distinct left key
questions.explanation: A Cartesian product pairs every left row with every right row.

questions.prompt: How many rows result from a cross join of four rows and five rows?
questions.explanation: A Cartesian product has the product of input cardinalities.

questions.prompt: Why should self-joins normally use aliases?
choices: To force all keys to become unique
To avoid every possible data shuffle
To distinguish references to the two roles of the same DataFrame
questions.explanation: Aliases make column references unambiguous; they do not change key cardinality.

questions.prompt: Which result does a left semi join produce when one left row matches five right rows?
choices: No rows unless the right side is unique
One copy of that left row
Five copies of that left row
questions.explanation: Semi joins test existence rather than returning every matching pair.

questions.prompt: What columns does a left anti join return?
choices: Only the join key and a count
Only columns from the left input
Only columns from the right input
questions.explanation: Anti joins filter the left input by absence of a match, retaining its schema.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of filtering a right-side column after a left join with right.status = 'active'?
choices: Unmatched rows are removed because their right status is null
The filter always preserves every unmatched left row
The filter turns every null into active
The filter changes all joins to cross joins
questions.explanation: A post-join predicate requiring a true right-side condition excludes null-extended unmatched rows.

questions.prompt: What does DataFrame.union do with duplicate rows?
choices: It raises an error whenever duplicates exist
questions.explanation: DataFrame.union behaves like UNION ALL in SQL with respect to duplicates.

questions.prompt: How does plain DataFrame.union align columns?
questions.explanation: Positional alignment can silently mix values when compatible columns are ordered differently.

questions.prompt: What is unionByName designed to change relative to union?
choices: It aligns corresponding columns by name
It joins rows by primary key
questions.explanation: unionByName addresses schema alignment, not deduplication or keyed row matching.

questions.prompt: What does allowMissingColumns=True do in unionByName?
choices: Deletes every field missing from either side
questions.explanation: The option permits name-aligned unions with missing columns by inserting nulls for absent fields.

questions.prompt: What are the resulting values of a and b in the second appended row?
questions.code:
left = spark.createDataFrame([(1, 2)], ["a", "b"])
right = spark.createDataFrame([(10, 20)], ["b", "a"])
left.unionByName(right)
questions.explanation: unionByName follows names even though the second input has reversed column order.

questions.prompt: For identical input rows repeated in both DataFrames, what does intersect return?
choices: Only rows unique to the left
Every repeated row from the left
questions.explanation: intersect returns distinct rows common to both inputs. intersectAll preserves multiplicity differently.

questions.prompt: If left has three copies of x and right has two copies of x, how many copies does intersectAll return?
questions.explanation: Multiset intersection retains the minimum multiplicity across the two inputs.

questions.prompt: If left has three copies of x and right has one copy of x, how many copies does exceptAll return?
questions.explanation: exceptAll subtracts matching multiplicities, leaving two copies here.

questions.prompt: Which operation is equivalent to EXCEPT DISTINCT rather than EXCEPT ALL?
questions.explanation: subtract returns distinct rows from the left that are absent from the right.

questions.prompt: What is a safe first step before a many-to-one enrichment join?
choices: Drop every left-side duplicate regardless of meaning
Verify uniqueness of the right-side business key
Assume the word dimension guarantees uniqueness
questions.explanation: Cardinality validation catches unintended row multiplication before it reaches downstream measures.

questions.prompt: Why can joining raw floating-point measures as keys be fragile?
choices: All floating-point joins become Cartesian products
Representation and rounding can make apparently similar values unequal
questions.explanation: Approximate numeric representation can differ across computations; stable identifiers or explicit normalization are usually better keys.

questions.prompt: Which call expresses a two-key name-based equality join?
questions.explanation: A list of names specifies equality on both shared fields. One comma-containing string is a single field name.

questions.prompt: What rows does a full outer join preserve?
choices: Only rows whose keys are null
Matched pairs plus unmatched rows from both inputs
questions.explanation: Full outer joins retain unmatched rows from either side, filling absent-side columns with null.

questions.prompt: After a join, why explicitly select and rename needed output fields?
choices: To guarantee no rows are lost
To produce a clear, unambiguous schema and avoid accidental duplicate names
To force every join to be one-to-one
questions.explanation: Projection makes the output contract clear; it does not repair an incorrect join relationship by itself.

questions.prompt: How does a window aggregation usually differ from groupBy aggregation?
choices: It automatically writes a new table
It retains each input row while adding an analytic result
It always reduces the dataset to one row
It can operate only on strings
questions.explanation: Window results are associated with input rows, preserving their detail unless another operation filters or aggregates them.

questions.prompt: What does Window.partitionBy("customer") define?
choices: A guarantee of one output file per customer
questions.explanation: The window partition defines which rows participate together in the analytic calculation.

questions.prompt: Which method applies a window specification to a compatible expression?
questions.explanation: Functions such as row_number and sum use over(window_spec) to become window expressions.

questions.prompt: What does row_number assign within an ordered window partition?
choices: A globally unique permanent event identifier
A shared number for every tie
questions.explanation: row_number numbers rows in the specified window order. Ties need additional ordering for deterministic assignment.

questions.prompt: For scores 100, 100, 90 in descending order, what rank values are produced?
questions.explanation: rank shares the tied rank and leaves a gap after the two tied rows.

questions.prompt: For scores 100, 100, 90 in descending order, what dense_rank values are produced?
questions.explanation: dense_rank assigns consecutive distinct rank values without gaps after ties.

questions.prompt: Which function is best for selecting exactly one record per key when a complete ordering is provided?
choices: rank followed by filtering to 1 in every case
dense_rank followed by filtering to 1 in every case
questions.explanation: row_number chooses one row. rank and dense_rank can retain multiple tied top rows.

questions.prompt: Why include event_id after event_time in the ordering for latest-record selection?
choices: To remove every null from every column
To convert the window into a groupBy
To break equal timestamps deterministically when event_id is unique
To make all event timestamps distinct automatically
questions.explanation: A unique tie-breaker makes the ordering complete without changing the timestamps themselves.

questions.prompt: What is prev for the first row of each customer under this expression?
questions.code: F.lag("amount", 1).over(Window.partitionBy("customer").orderBy("event_id"))
questions.explanation: lag returns its default, which is null, when no preceding row exists.

questions.prompt: What does the third argument specify in lag("amount", 1, 0)?
choices: The fallback when no row exists at that offset
A replacement for every null amount encountered
questions.explanation: The default handles missing offset rows; it does not generally replace null values in an existing preceding row.

questions.prompt: Which function accesses a following row in the window order?
questions.explanation: lead looks forward; lag looks backward relative to the current row.

questions.prompt: For amounts 5, 8, 2 ordered by unique sequence, what are running sums using unboundedPreceding through currentRow?
questions.explanation: Each row includes itself and all earlier rows in the partition.

questions.prompt: Which frame expresses the current row and previous two row positions?
questions.explanation: Negative row offsets refer to preceding rows, and zero includes the current row.

questions.prompt: Are the endpoints of rowsBetween included in the frame?
choices: Only the lower endpoint is inclusive
Only the upper endpoint is inclusive
questions.explanation: Both boundaries participate, so rowsBetween(-1, 1) covers up to three rows.

questions.prompt: What is the key distinction between rowsBetween and rangeBetween?
choices: Rows supports only strings; range supports only arrays
Rows creates rows; range deletes rows
Rows uses positions; range uses ordering-value distances
questions.explanation: A value-based range can include all peers with the same order value, whereas row offsets count positions.

questions.prompt: Two rows have order value 10. What does rangeBetween(0, 0) include for either row?
questions.explanation: A zero-distance range includes peers whose ordering value equals the current one.

questions.prompt: Which explicit frame calculates a full-partition sum while keeping an order specification?
questions.explanation: Unbounded boundaries include every row in the partition, not only the running prefix.

questions.prompt: Why can last_value over an ordered default frame return the current row's value rather than the partition's final value?
choices: The frame may stop at the current order value instead of the partition end
The final value is inaccessible in Spark
questions.explanation: The function sees its frame, not automatically the whole partition. Specify an unbounded-following frame for the final partition value.

questions.prompt: Which import supplies the Window specification builder?
questions.explanation: Window is part of pyspark.sql, while ranking and aggregate functions are in pyspark.sql.functions.

questions.prompt: What does this calculation add to every employee row?
questions.code: F.avg("salary").over(Window.partitionBy("department"))
choices: The employee's previous salary by default
The average salary in that employee's department
One row for each department only
questions.explanation: The partition groups department peers, and the aggregate is evaluated over that partition.

questions.prompt: Which calculation obtains a row's difference from its department average?
questions.explanation: A window average preserves each salary row so that a row-wise difference can be calculated.

questions.prompt: What happens to window numbering when the partition key changes to another customer?
choices: The sequence restarts within that customer's partition
It must continue globally without restarting
It uses the prior customer's final value as the start
It becomes null for every later customer
questions.explanation: Window partitioning defines independent analytic groups.

questions.prompt: Why is a window with no partitionBy potentially expensive on a very large dataset?
choices: It automatically becomes a million partitions
It calculates only the first input row
It describes one global analytic partition
questions.explanation: A global window can require moving all rows into one analytic partition, limiting parallelism.

questions.prompt: What does this filter accomplish when ts and id define a total descending order per key?
questions.code:
w = Window.partitionBy("key").orderBy(F.col("ts").desc(), F.col("id").desc())
df.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1")
choices: Keeps the earliest row per key
Keeps the latest single row per key according to that order
Keeps every tied latest timestamp regardless of id
questions.explanation: Descending ordering followed by row_number=1 selects the first row in that complete ordering.

questions.prompt: Why should a moving-average requirement specify whether the window means rows or elapsed time?
choices: Irregular event spacing makes a fixed row count different from a fixed time interval
Every sequence has equally spaced events
Spark always infers the intended business window
questions.explanation: The last three events may span minutes or days. Translate the business time rule into the appropriate ordering and frame.

questions.prompt: For ordered values 4, 6, 10, what is lag(value, 1, -1) on the row with 6?
questions.explanation: The prior row exists and contains 4, so the fallback is not used.

questions.prompt: For ordered values 4, 6, 10, what is lead(value, 1, -1) on the row with 10?
questions.explanation: There is no next row, so lead returns the explicitly supplied default -1.

questions.prompt: What does ntile(4) do over an ordered partition?
choices: Computes the fourth power of each value
Assigns rows to four approximately equal-size numbered buckets
questions.explanation: ntile divides the ordered rows into the requested number of buckets as evenly as possible.

questions.prompt: When using a finite rangeBetween with numeric offsets, why must you inspect the ordering expression?
choices: The offsets are Python slice endpoints
The offsets are measured in the ordering expression's value units and have type/column restrictions
Any number of string ordering columns is automatically valid
questions.explanation: Range frames are value-based; a timestamp converted to seconds and an integer sequence imply different meanings.

questions.prompt: Which ordering explicitly places null scores after non-null scores in descending order?
questions.explanation: desc_nulls_last states both direction and null placement, making a ranking rule easier to review.

questions.prompt: Which nested type stores named fields such as latitude and longitude together?
