To isolate artifacts and avoid depending on or damaging real data
To guarantee all file writes are instantaneous
questions.explanation: Temporary fixtures make tests reproducible and cleanable. They do not eliminate filesystem semantics.

questions.prompt: Why is 'the job finished' alone an insufficient successful-ingestion log?
choices: Only exceptions are allowed in production logs
It lacks counts and context needed to detect partial or unexpected processing
A success message must always be ERROR
questions.explanation: Include relevant counts, identifiers and duration so completion can be compared with expectations. No exception does not prove complete input coverage.

questions.prompt: Which assertion checks object identity rather than value equality?
questions.explanation: assertIs tests whether references point to the same object. Most transformation result checks need equality instead.

questions.prompt: A mocked writer is called for an invalid record despite the expected validation error. Which assertion detects this unwanted side effect?
questions.explanation: assert_not_called checks that validation prevented the storage operation. Resetting a mock only clears history and does not assert behavior.

questions.prompt: Which executor uses worker threads?
questions.explanation: ThreadPoolExecutor runs callables in threads. Futures represent results rather than defining their execution resources.

questions.prompt: What does executor.submit(fn, arg) return?
choices: A generator of all executor results
A Future representing the scheduled call
The final result synchronously in every case
questions.explanation: The Future tracks completion and exposes the result or exception later. Submission itself does not prove successful execution.

questions.prompt: If a submitted function raises ValueError, what normally happens when future.result() is called?
choices: The exception is raised to the caller
The exception becomes a string automatically
questions.explanation: Future.result propagates the worker exception. Ignoring Futures can hide failures from application logic.

questions.prompt: What order does executor.map normally yield results in?
choices: Sorted by the result's numeric value
The order of the input iterable
questions.explanation: map preserves input order, which can make consumption wait for an earlier slow task. as_completed serves a different ordering need.

questions.prompt: Which utility yields Futures as they complete?
questions.explanation: as_completed iterates completed Futures without preserving submission order. Inspect each result to surface errors.

questions.prompt: For conventional CPython 3.11, why may threads not speed up CPU-heavy pure Python bytecode?
choices: The CPU is disabled while threads exist
The GIL limits simultaneous Python bytecode execution
Threads are unable to share memory
Every thread runs on a remote machine
questions.explanation: Threads can still help overlap I/O, and native extensions may release the GIL. The workload determines the benefit.

questions.prompt: Which executor is often appropriate for independent CPU-heavy pure Python tasks that can be serialized?
choices: One thread per byte of input
A single Future with no executor
questions.explanation: Processes can use multiple cores for Python execution. Serialization and process overhead must be weighed against task size.

questions.prompt: Why must functions and arguments submitted to ProcessPoolExecutor be picklable?
choices: The executor stores everything as CSV
Python processes share one stack automatically
Pickling is required only to print logs
They must cross process boundaries through serialization
questions.explanation: Process workers do not share ordinary Python object references. Serialization constraints affect what can be submitted.

questions.prompt: Why put process-pool startup under if __name__ == '__main__': in a portable script?
choices: To make every function global automatically
To prevent any imports in workers
To avoid rerunning process-creation code when worker processes import the module
questions.explanation: Spawn-based startup imports the main module. A main guard prevents recursive pool creation during that import.

questions.prompt: A task in a one-worker ThreadPoolExecutor waits on another task submitted to that same pool. What can happen?
choices: Deadlock because the only worker is occupied waiting
The second task always steals the worker instantly
The pool automatically grows without limit
questions.explanation: Nested waits can exhaust available workers. Avoid task dependencies that require resources held by the waiting task.

questions.prompt: Does future.cancel() forcibly stop a function that is already running?
choices: No; cancellation usually succeeds only before running begins
Yes; it kills the worker process immediately in all executors
Yes; it rolls back external writes automatically
Only if the function returns a string
questions.explanation: Cancellation is not a transactional undo or general forced interruption. Running work needs cooperative stopping or other lifecycle design.

questions.prompt: What does calling an async def function initially return?
questions.explanation: The coroutine must be awaited or scheduled to execute. Creating it alone does not run the whole operation.

questions.prompt: Why is time.sleep(5) problematic inside an asyncio coroutine on the event-loop thread?
choices: It blocks that thread and delays other coroutines
questions.explanation: A blocking sleep does not yield to the event loop. await asyncio.sleep(5) cooperatively suspends the coroutine.

questions.prompt: Which expression cooperatively waits without blocking the event-loop thread?
questions.explanation: asyncio.sleep suspends the task so other ready tasks can run. Busy waiting and synchronous input block progress.

questions.prompt: What does asyncio.create_task(coro()) do?
choices: Schedules the coroutine to run as an asyncio Task
Executes it in a new process
Converts it into a blocking function
questions.explanation: A Task schedules cooperative execution on the running loop. It is not an operating-system thread.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism can bound concurrent in-flight API requests among asyncio tasks?
choices: An unbounded list of create_task calls alone
questions.explanation: A semaphore controls admission to a limited resource. Choose a limit consistent with service capacity and memory.

questions.prompt: What is a main benefit of asyncio.TaskGroup in Python 3.11?
choices: It removes the need to await anything
It shares database transactions across processes
It scopes related tasks and coordinates waiting and failure handling
It makes blocking calls nonblocking automatically
questions.explanation: TaskGroup provides structured task lifetime management. Work inside tasks still needs appropriate asynchronous operations.

questions.prompt: When one task in an asyncio.TaskGroup fails with a non-cancellation exception, what generally happens to its unfinished sibling tasks?
choices: They are cancelled and the group waits for them before raising grouped errors
They are abandoned permanently without cleanup
questions.explanation: TaskGroup coordinates cancellation and waits for task shutdown. Coroutines should preserve cancellation behavior while cleaning up.

questions.prompt: What does asyncio.to_thread help with in an async application?
choices: Running a suitable blocking I/O function without blocking the event-loop thread
Converting every CPU-bound function into unlimited parallel execution
Starting a new event loop for every await
Making a database write automatically idempotent
questions.explanation: to_thread offloads the synchronous call to a thread. The GIL and the function's thread-safety still matter.

questions.prompt: Why should a coroutine usually re-raise CancelledError after cleanup?
choices: So every error becomes a successful result
Because cancellation always means data corruption
So cancellation can propagate through task-management machinery
questions.explanation: Suppressing cancellation can interfere with timeouts and structured concurrency. Use finally for cleanup and preserve the intended cancellation contract.

questions.prompt: Two threads perform a read-modify-write update on shared state. What should protect the invariant?
choices: An appropriate lock or another synchronization design
The assumption that every multi-step operation is atomic because of the GIL
questions.explanation: The GIL does not make arbitrary sequences of operations atomic. Synchronize the whole invariant-preserving operation.

questions.prompt: Why use queue.Queue between producer and consumer threads?
choices: It provides synchronized item transfer and optional bounded capacity
It guarantees every item is valid JSON
questions.explanation: Queue coordinates safe transfer, while worker lifecycle and data validation remain application responsibilities.

questions.prompt: What can a bounded queue provide when producers outpace consumers?
choices: Backpressure by blocking or rejecting additional puts according to the API used
A guarantee that consumers never fail
questions.explanation: Bounded capacity limits buffered work. The application must choose how to handle blocking, timeout or full-queue conditions.

questions.prompt: What must a worker normally call after completing an item so Queue.join can observe completion?
questions.explanation: task_done decrements the unfinished-task count. join waits for that count to reach zero, not merely for the queue to look empty.

questions.prompt: Why add jitter to exponential retry backoff across many workers?
choices: To bypass a service's rate limit
To guarantee the next request succeeds
questions.explanation: Random variation spreads retry timing. It should complement bounded retries and respect service limits.

questions.prompt: A request times out after the server may have committed a write. What should guide the retry?
choices: An idempotency key or reconciliation of the operation's outcome
Assume timeout proves the write never happened
Always generate a new event identifier
questions.explanation: A lost response leaves the outcome uncertain. Stable operation identity helps avoid duplicate effects.

questions.prompt: Which failure is normally a poor candidate for blind transient retries?
choices: A documented throttling response with retry guidance
questions.explanation: Invalid data will usually fail again unchanged. Classify failures before applying retries.

questions.prompt: Why bound both retry attempts and total elapsed time?
choices: To ensure every external system becomes exactly-once
To eliminate the need for logging
To limit resource consumption and avoid indefinite stalled work
questions.explanation: A retry budget makes failure behavior predictable. It does not itself guarantee successful or duplicate-free execution.

questions.prompt: What order does asyncio.gather normally return successful results in?
choices: The order of the supplied awaitables
questions.explanation: gather preserves argument order in its result list. Scheduling and actual completion order can differ.

questions.prompt: A worker pool submits a million large payloads before consuming results. What production concern is most immediate?
choices: The pool cannot accept more tasks than workers
Unbounded pending work can exhaust memory despite a small worker count
A small pool guarantees constant total memory automatically
Every payload is immediately written to disk by the executor
questions.explanation: Worker count bounds simultaneous execution, not necessarily queued inputs. Use batching or bounded submission.

questions.prompt: What does a sequence of ordinary DataFrame select and filter transformations primarily construct before an action?
choices: One permanent table per method call
A fixed number of executor processes
questions.explanation: DataFrame transformations describe computation. Spark evaluates the required plan when an action demands results.

questions.prompt: Which operation is an action on a DataFrame?
questions.explanation: count requires a result from the data. The other operations create transformed DataFrame plans.

questions.prompt: Why can timing only df.filter(...) misrepresent pipeline performance?
choices: It mostly measures plan construction rather than execution of the filtered result
filter always reads every byte twice
questions.explanation: A meaningful benchmark must execute an action and account for caching and input conditions. Lazy construction is not equivalent to processing the dataset.

questions.prompt: Which plan feature most directly signals repartitioning data across executors for a relational operation?
questions.explanation: A shuffle exchange redistributes records to satisfy partitioning requirements. Projection and aliases do not inherently require that movement.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a logical and a physical query plan?
choices: The logical plan describes relational intent; the physical plan selects execution operators
The logical plan contains only Python source and the physical plan contains only filenames
The logical plan executes after the physical plan finishes
Only the logical plan can represent joins
questions.explanation: Physical planning chooses implementations for the intended operations. The optimizer can transform the logical structure before those choices.

questions.prompt: A Parquet query uses only three of a hundred columns. Which optimization can reduce input bytes?
questions.explanation: Columnar storage can read the required columns rather than all columns. Collecting first moves unnecessary data to the driver.

questions.prompt: A table is partitioned on event_date and a query filters that column. What should be inspected to confirm directory skipping?
choices: Only the number of selected output columns
Partition filters in the scan plan
questions.explanation: Partition pruning can avoid reading irrelevant directories. Its presence should be confirmed from the plan and scan metrics.

questions.prompt: Why can a built-in Spark expression outperform an equivalent scalar Python UDF?
choices: It can remain visible to Spark optimization and avoid some Python execution overhead
It forces all data onto the driver
questions.explanation: Built-ins expose semantics to the engine and avoid some cross-runtime cost. The actual benefit still depends on the expression and workload.

questions.prompt: A narrow dependency means each child partition depends on what?
choices: A limited set of parent partitions without all-to-all redistribution
Every parent partition for every row
Only data stored on the driver
questions.explanation: Narrow dependencies can often be pipelined. Wide dependencies generally require data redistribution.

questions.prompt: Why does reduceByKey often move less data than groupByKey followed by summing in an RDD pipeline?
choices: It collects values on the driver first
It can combine values locally before the shuffle
questions.explanation: Map-side combination reduces transferred records for associative reductions. A shuffle may still be necessary.

questions.prompt: A DataFrame is used by two actions without persistence. What may happen?
choices: Spark converts it into a local Python list
Its upstream computation may execute again
The first action always permanently caches it
questions.explanation: A DataFrame variable holds a plan, not a promise of stored results. Persist when measured reuse justifies storage.

questions.prompt: Why is one Python transformation not necessarily one Spark stage?
choices: Every action has exactly one stage
Spark can pipeline compatible work and introduce stage boundaries around exchanges
Stages are determined solely by function names
Every transformation is a separate application
questions.explanation: Execution structure follows dependencies and planning, not a one-to-one mapping to API calls. Inspect the DAG and SQL plan.

questions.prompt: A query pushes a supported filter into a data source. What is the intended benefit?
choices: Reduce data returned from the source or decoded by Spark
Force all records through a Python UDF
Remove the need for the predicate entirely
questions.explanation: Pushdown can reduce work at the source, but Spark may still apply residual filters. Support depends on the connector and predicate.

questions.prompt: A filter wraps a partition column in an opaque Python UDF. What optimization concern should be investigated?
choices: The UDF guarantees more accurate partition statistics
The filter must automatically become a broadcast join
The engine may be unable to use the expression for partition pruning
questions.explanation: Opaque expressions can hide useful semantics. Compare the scan plan with an equivalent built-in predicate where possible.

questions.prompt: Why is explain output useful before forcing a join strategy?
choices: It executes every possible alternative and picks the fastest empirically
It guarantees no data skew exists
It shows the chosen strategy and relevant exchanges
It proves the query returns correct business results
questions.explanation: The plan reveals engine choices but does not replace correctness checks or runtime metrics. Use it to frame a measured optimization.

questions.prompt: Which Spark UI view connects SQL/DataFrame queries to their execution plans and metrics?
questions.explanation: The SQL view relates query operators and execution details. Other tabs answer configuration, storage or stage-specific questions.

questions.prompt: What is lineage used for in Spark fault recovery?
choices: Recomputing lost partitions from their dependencies
Restoring arbitrary external side effects automatically
questions.explanation: Lineage describes how data can be recomputed. External writes require their own retry-safe design.

questions.prompt: Why should side effects inside transformations be treated cautiously?
choices: Transformations always execute exactly once per row
Spark forbids all network access from workers
Each side effect is automatically transactional
Tasks may be retried or recomputed, repeating the side effect
questions.explanation: Execution retries can repeat code. Use supported sinks and explicit idempotency for external effects.

questions.prompt: An adaptive plan changes after execution. Why can a pre-action explain differ from the final executed plan?
choices: The Python source file is rewritten
Spark randomly chooses a new logical query
AQE can use runtime statistics to revise eligible execution choices
The DataFrame becomes mutable during count
questions.explanation: AQE adapts physical choices using observed statistics. Compare initial and final plans when diagnosing adaptive behavior.

questions.prompt: Why should a production aggregation explicitly define how null keys and null values are treated?
choices: SQL null semantics can affect grouping and aggregate results differently
Nulls always cause Spark to crash
Every aggregate treats null exactly like zero
questions.explanation: Grouping and aggregates have specific null behavior. Business rules may require normalization or separate quality checks.

questions.prompt: A pipeline repeatedly calls count inside a loop merely to decide whether to log progress. What is the likely cost?
choices: Repeated actions can trigger repeated jobs
count is always metadata-only for every DataFrame
The loop necessarily shares one cached result
questions.explanation: Actions can be expensive. Use planned observations or necessary result metrics instead of repeatedly scanning solely for logs.

questions.prompt: Why can selecting necessary columns before a wide operation reduce shuffle cost?
choices: It changes all joins to broadcast joins
It eliminates the need for serialization
Narrower records may require fewer bytes to redistribute
questions.explanation: Reducing row width can reduce network and memory use, provided the removed columns are not needed later. The optimizer may already perform equivalent pruning.

questions.prompt: A filter is nondeterministic. Why might the optimizer be more constrained about moving it?
choices: It is automatically executed only on the driver
It forces every input to be cached
Moving it can change evaluation behavior and results
Nondeterministic filters always evaluate to false
questions.explanation: Optimization must preserve semantics. Reordering nondeterministic expressions can change which values are evaluated or retained.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with assuming df.show(5) has validated every record in a large input?
choices: show sorts all columns by default
It displays a limited result and may not exercise all data or paths
show always displays exactly five partitions
show checks every business constraint automatically
questions.explanation: A small display is an inspection aid, not a full validation action. Design explicit checks for the complete dataset.

questions.prompt: A global orderBy is added only to make an intermediate display pleasant. What cost can it introduce?
choices: A distributed sort and associated data movement
Only a local string formatting operation
Automatic compression of all input files
questions.explanation: Global ordering is a substantive distributed operation. Avoid carrying it through a pipeline unless the result contract requires it.

questions.prompt: Does increasing the number of executor cores always reduce the runtime of a stage?
choices: Yes; runtime always scales inversely with cores
Yes; Spark automatically divides every single record
No; Spark can never execute tasks in parallel
No; partition count, skew, I/O and scheduling overhead can limit gains
questions.explanation: Available parallel work and resource bottlenecks determine scaling. A single large skewed partition may remain the critical path.

questions.prompt: Why is an explain plan alone insufficient to identify the slowest stage?
choices: It is always unrelated to the executed query
It describes execution structure but runtime data sizes and durations matter
questions.explanation: Plans and runtime metrics are complementary. An operator's cost depends on actual volumes, skew and resources.

questions.prompt: Which measurement most directly distinguishes a task straggler from uniformly slow tasks?
choices: The distribution of task durations within a stage
The length of the application name
questions.explanation: A few extreme task durations suggest imbalance or localized problems. Uniform slowness points toward a different class of bottleneck.

questions.prompt: What does df.explain(mode='extended') add beyond a simple physical-plan display?
choices: Logical-plan stages as well as the physical plan
A complete copy of all source rows
questions.explanation: Extended explain exposes parsed, analyzed and optimized logical representations plus the physical plan. It helps trace transformations through planning.

questions.prompt: A tuning change reduces shuffle bytes but makes end-to-end latency worse. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: Shuffle bytes are the only valid performance metric
The change should be deployed because one metric improved
The optimization must be evaluated against the overall workload objective and new bottlenecks
questions.explanation: Performance work balances multiple costs. Reduced network traffic can be offset by extra CPU, skew or reduced parallelism.

questions.prompt: What is a Spark partition primarily used as during distributed execution?
choices: A Python thread owned by the driver
A unit of data processed by tasks
A guaranteed one-to-one mapping to an executor for the entire application
questions.explanation: Partitions organize distributed work. Executors can process many partitions over time.

questions.prompt: How does DataFrame.repartition generally differ from coalesce when reducing partition count?
choices: repartition redistributes through a shuffle; coalesce can merge partitions without a full shuffle
coalesce always globally sorts the data
questions.explanation: Repartition can improve distribution at shuffle cost. Coalesce commonly avoids that shuffle but may preserve imbalance.

questions.prompt: A large dataset is coalesced to one partition before writing. What is the main risk?
choices: A single task becomes a throughput and memory bottleneck
The output becomes a single scalar value
The schema is automatically inferred again
questions.explanation: Concentrating output on one partition reduces parallelism. A single-file requirement should be weighed against dataset size.

questions.prompt: Does repartition(100, 'customer_id') guarantee exactly equal row counts in every partition?
choices: Yes; Spark splits every key evenly across all partitions
Yes; each partition always gets exactly one percent
Only when customer_id is a string
No; key frequencies and hashing can produce uneven counts
questions.explanation: Hash partitioning groups equal keys together. Uneven key frequency can produce skew.

questions.prompt: A single key represents half the input. Why may simply increasing hash partition count fail to fix its aggregation straggler?
choices: Hashing stops working above ten partitions
The driver performs every aggregation locally
All rows for that key still map to one hash partition
questions.explanation: More buckets do not split one key across buckets. A targeted strategy is needed for hot-key work.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most strongly suggests skew in a join stage?
choices: The schema contains a string field
A few tasks have much larger shuffle input and duration than the median
Every task has nearly identical input and duration
questions.explanation: Uneven data and time distributions point toward imbalance. Confirm the responsible keys or partitions before changing the plan.

questions.prompt: When can broadcasting a join relation be a good choice?
choices: It is genuinely small enough for relevant memory budgets and the join supports the strategy
It is merely smaller than the other relation, regardless of absolute size
It has more columns than the other relation
It is always the left relation
questions.explanation: Relative size alone is insufficient. Broadcast feasibility depends on absolute runtime size and supported join semantics.

questions.prompt: Why is a small compressed Parquet file not sufficient proof that a relation is safe to broadcast?
choices: Parquet compression guarantees zero memory use
Every compressed file is ineligible for broadcast
Its decoded and hashed runtime representation can be much larger
questions.explanation: Memory sizing must consider the materialized relation, not just compressed storage bytes. Nested or wide records can expand substantially.

questions.prompt: Does a BROADCAST hint guarantee Spark uses the requested strategy for every join type?
choices: Yes; it converts every join to an inner join
No; Spark ignores all hints unconditionally
No; strategy support and planning constraints still apply
Yes; hints override all semantic constraints
questions.explanation: Hints influence planning but cannot make every strategy support every join type. Inspect the resulting plan.

questions.prompt: What does spark.sql.shuffle.partitions configure for many SQL shuffle operations?
choices: The maximum number of rows in a DataFrame
The maximum number of source files in the filesystem
questions.explanation: This setting influences shuffle parallelism. AQE and specific operations may adjust the final partitioning.

questions.prompt: What input does AQE use that static planning may not know accurately?
choices: Runtime statistics from executed query stages
Only the wall-clock day of the week
questions.explanation: Runtime sizes help AQE revise eligible physical choices. This does not mean it can rewrite arbitrary application logic.

questions.prompt: Which is an AQE capability in Spark 3.5.7?
choices: Making all Python UDFs native expressions
questions.explanation: AQE can merge small shuffle partitions based on runtime information. Its scope is query execution optimization.

questions.prompt: Under Spark 3.5.7 skew-join detection, why are both relative and absolute partition-size thresholds useful?
choices: They guarantee a key is unique
They distinguish unusually large partitions that are also large enough to matter
They force every partition to have identical row counts
questions.explanation: A partition must exceed the configured factor relative to the median and the absolute size threshold to meet the documented skew criterion.

questions.prompt: What is the intent of salting a hot join key when implemented correctly?
choices: Replace every key with the same constant
Spread its work across additional subkeys while preserving join results
Encrypt the key so Spark cannot inspect it
Drop all records for the hot key
questions.explanation: Salting changes data distribution. Matching-side replication or compatible key treatment must preserve the original semantics.

questions.prompt: A salted aggregation computes partial sums by (key, salt). What final step is needed for the original sum per key?
choices: Aggregate the partial sums again by the original key
Average the partial sums regardless of counts
Collect every raw row to the driver
questions.explanation: The second aggregation combines the salted partial results. This works for decomposable operations such as sums.

questions.prompt: Why is averaging per-partition averages usually wrong when partition sizes differ?
choices: Every partition must contain one row
Averages always require sorting by key
The partial averages need weighting by their counts
questions.explanation: Carry sum and count, then divide total sum by total count. Unweighted averages give equal weight to unequal groups.

questions.prompt: What tradeoff can result from choosing far too many shuffle partitions for a small dataset?
choices: Automatic elimination of all file opens
Mandatory use of a broadcast nested loop join
Scheduling overhead and many tiny tasks
Guaranteed out-of-memory from one giant partition
questions.explanation: Tiny tasks may spend more time in coordination than useful work. AQE can help in eligible plans but should be verified.

questions.prompt: What tradeoff can result from choosing far too few shuffle partitions for a large dataset?
choices: Large tasks, memory pressure and limited parallelism
questions.explanation: Large partitions can increase per-task resource demand and leave available cores unused. Tune against actual volumes.

questions.prompt: Does repartitionByRange imply that rows within every partition are already fully sorted for consumers?
choices: No; range partitioning and in-partition sorting are separate requirements
Yes; it guarantees every possible later orderBy is free
Yes; it sorts every column descending
No; it disables range boundaries entirely
questions.explanation: Range partitioning organizes ranges, while explicit sorting may still be needed. Specify the ordering contract separately.

questions.prompt: A dimension table grows dramatically over time. What should a previously forced broadcast join be reevaluated against?
choices: Only the fact that it is called a dimension
The length of its table name
Current decoded size, memory use and observed plan/runtime
questions.explanation: A once-safe strategy can become unsafe as data changes. Monitor assumptions that a manual hint depends on.

questions.prompt: Why can broadcasting both large sides of a join be a poor tuning approach?
choices: Spark always keeps both sides only on disk
Hints do not remove memory limits or the need for a feasible build side
Broadcast hints compress every object without overhead
questions.explanation: Join strategy must respect relation sizes and support. More hints do not substitute for a viable plan.

questions.prompt: A filter reduces a dimension from millions of rows to a few hundred. What potential join optimization should be inspected?
choices: Collecting the fact table to Python
Broadcasting the filtered relation when safe
Broadcasting the unfiltered relation first in all cases
questions.explanation: The post-filter size may make a broadcast strategy suitable. Verify optimizer placement and runtime size.

questions.prompt: Why can pre-aggregation before a join improve performance when it preserves required semantics?
choices: It can reduce the number of records participating in the join
It always preserves all possible downstream detail
It eliminates the need to validate join keys
questions.explanation: Reducing rows can lower shuffle and join work. Check that the aggregation level still supports the intended result.

questions.prompt: A join unexpectedly multiplies row counts. Which issue should be checked before performance tuning?
choices: Only the number of output files
Duplicate join keys causing many-to-many matches
questions.explanation: Cardinality explosions can be a data-model or correctness issue. Resource changes do not fix an unintended many-to-many join.

questions.prompt: Which setting enables the umbrella AQE feature in Spark 3.5.7?
questions.explanation: AQE is controlled by spark.sql.adaptive.enabled. Its individual optimization rules also have settings and eligibility conditions.

questions.prompt: If AQE coalesces shuffle partitions, is the final number always identical to spark.sql.shuffle.partitions?
choices: No; it always chooses exactly one
No; AQE can choose a different final number based on runtime data
Yes; the setting is an immutable final count
questions.explanation: The shuffle setting can be an initial count. Adaptive coalescing changes eligible downstream partitioning.

questions.prompt: A workload has many tiny input files. Which concern exists even if their total bytes are modest?
choices: Every file automatically becomes a separate executor
The data must be duplicated in Python
Parquet cannot read more than one file
questions.explanation: Small-file overhead can dominate useful processing. Compaction and scan configuration should be considered with the storage layout.

questions.prompt: Why should output partition columns usually avoid extremely high cardinality such as a unique event ID?
choices: They guarantee better compression for every workload
They make all downstream queries metadata-only
They can create excessive directories and small files
questions.explanation: Storage partitioning should align with access patterns and practical file sizes. Unique keys usually fragment the layout excessively.

questions.prompt: A skew fix replicates the small side for salt values. What cost must be measured?
choices: A mandatory loss of all null values
A guarantee that every join becomes faster
Extra rows and memory/network work from replication
Only the number of Python imports
questions.explanation: Salting exchanges one imbalance cost for extra work. Validate both correctness and end-to-end performance.

questions.prompt: What is the best basis for choosing a partition count for a production workload?
choices: Always one partition per business entity
Representative data size, task metrics, resources and target file sizes
A universal number copied from an unrelated benchmark
questions.explanation: Partition tuning depends on workload and cluster constraints. Recheck when volume or key distribution changes.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of caching a Spark DataFrame?
choices: Reuse computed data across later operations
Guarantee every query needs no shuffle
Permanently save data as a governed table
Convert it to a Python dictionary
questions.explanation: Caching avoids some repeated computation when data is reused. It is an execution optimization, not a durable data-management contract.

questions.prompt: When are cached DataFrame partitions generally populated?
choices: Immediately when a Python variable is assigned
When actions compute the required partitions
questions.explanation: Caching is generally lazy. Actions materialize the partitions they need, so a limited action may not populate everything.

questions.prompt: Which operation releases a persisted DataFrame from Spark storage?
questions.explanation: unpersist removes its persistence request and stored blocks. Dropping a column creates a different logical projection.

questions.prompt: Why can caching a DataFrame used only once make a workload slower?
choices: A one-use DataFrame cannot be cached
Materialization and storage overhead may provide no reuse benefit
questions.explanation: Cache only when avoided recomputation justifies its costs. One-time pipelines often gain nothing from it.

questions.prompt: Which Spark UI tab helps inspect persisted datasets and their cached partition coverage?
questions.explanation: The Storage tab shows persisted data and storage details. Use it to verify actual coverage instead of assuming every partition is cached.

questions.prompt: What can happen to a cached partition that is lost with an executor?
choices: The application always returns silent zeros
Every cached partition is automatically copied to the driver
Spark can recompute it from lineage when possible
questions.explanation: Persistence is not a replacement for durable storage. Recomputability depends on lineage and available input data.

questions.prompt: How does reliable checkpointing differ conceptually from ordinary caching?
choices: It always keeps all data only in executor memory
It guarantees external writes become transactional
It can truncate lineage using data stored in a reliable checkpoint location
questions.explanation: Checkpointing changes the recovery dependency structure. Caching mainly reuses data while lineage remains relevant.

questions.prompt: Why is localCheckpoint less reliable than a checkpoint written to a reliable distributed filesystem?
choices: It stores every row in the driver log
It relies on executor-local storage and can be lost with executors
It always uses JSON rather than Parquet
questions.explanation: Local checkpointing trades reliability for reduced overhead. Executor loss can invalidate the local checkpoint data.

questions.prompt: Why can collecting a huge DataFrame fail even when the cluster has abundant executor RAM?
choices: The complete collected result must fit in driver memory
collect automatically distributes the Python list over executors
Executor RAM is always transferred to the driver
questions.explanation: Driver and executor memory are separate resources. Distributed capacity does not make an unbounded local result safe.

questions.prompt: Which operation is more appropriate for inspecting a small bounded sample than collect?
choices: take(n) with a suitable small n
questions.explanation: take limits the returned rows. Slicing after collecting still transfers the entire result first.

questions.prompt: Why can a local iterator still create memory pressure even though it does not collect all rows at once?
choices: Individual partitions or downstream accumulation can still be large
Iterators always cache the full dataset by definition
It moves execution into one SQL transaction
questions.explanation: Incremental consumption reduces one risk but does not guarantee constant memory under every partitioning or consumer pattern.

questions.prompt: What does shuffle spill to disk indicate?
choices: Intermediate data was written to disk when memory was insufficient or managed limits required it
The driver has completed all work
questions.explanation: Spilling can allow a task to complete with limited memory. Heavy spill may identify an optimization opportunity.

questions.prompt: High task garbage-collection time most directly suggests investigating what?
choices: The CSV delimiter in every case
Memory pressure and object allocation patterns
questions.explanation: GC consumes time reclaiming memory. Large object populations, pressure and representation choices can contribute.

questions.prompt: Why can increasing executor heap fail to solve a Python worker memory problem?
choices: Heap size controls all machine memory without limits
Python worker and other non-heap overhead may require separate resources
Python workers always live inside the JVM heap only
questions.explanation: Understand the process and container memory layout. Heap, overhead and Python memory are not interchangeable budgets.

questions.prompt: A stage has high shuffle read time but low computation time. What bottleneck should be investigated first?
choices: Data movement and shuffle fetch behavior
questions.explanation: Shuffle-heavy waiting points toward network, disk, partitioning or fetch issues. Confirm with metrics and logs.

questions.prompt: What does the Spark History Server need to reconstruct an application's UI after it ends?
choices: Only a screenshot of the driver console
questions.explanation: Event logging preserves execution events for later inspection. Enable and retain it according to operational needs.

questions.prompt: Which Spark configuration enables event logging?
questions.explanation: Event logging supports after-the-fact history inspection. A suitable event-log directory and retention policy are also needed.

questions.prompt: Why compare executor metrics rather than looking only at total application duration?
choices: Executor metrics automatically correct bad data
All executors must have identical metrics
They help distinguish skew, GC, I/O and resource imbalance
Total duration always identifies the exact faulty line
questions.explanation: Aggregate duration hides where time is spent. Per-executor and per-task evidence narrows the cause.

questions.prompt: A DataFrame was cached before a selective filter used by every consumer. What alternative may reduce storage cost?
choices: Cache the reusable filtered projection if it matches all consumers' needs
questions.explanation: Store the smallest useful reusable result. Check whether other consumers need rows or columns removed by the filter.

questions.prompt: Why is a warm-cache benchmark insufficient to predict first-run latency?
choices: It omits input reading and initial materialization costs
Warm caches are always slower than cold reads
questions.explanation: Measure the conditions users actually experience. Report cache state alongside performance results.

questions.prompt: A task processes a single extremely large partition and fails with memory pressure. What targeted change may help?
choices: Cache the same oversized partition repeatedly
Increase appropriate parallelism or redesign the skewed work
questions.explanation: Reducing per-task work can address memory pressure. Merely adding storage may worsen contention.

questions.prompt: Why can many concurrent tasks per executor increase memory pressure?
choices: More cores always reduce per-executor memory needs
Each active task may need execution buffers and working memory
questions.explanation: Concurrency multiplies active working sets. Balance executor cores, memory and partition size together.

questions.prompt: What is a reason to call unpersist(blocking=True) before a memory-intensive next phase?
choices: Make unpersist populate the cache first
Wait for block removal to finish before proceeding
Force the next query to use one partition
Guarantee all input files are deleted
questions.explanation: Blocking removal can make the storage-release boundary explicit. It does not control every other memory allocation.

questions.prompt: A job is slow only on its first action after startup. Which cost should be considered?
choices: A guarantee that its algorithm is incorrect
The assumption that every action is identical
questions.explanation: Startup and warm-up can differ from steady state. Separate these costs when designing benchmarks.

questions.prompt: Why is caching a nondeterministic computation a semantic consideration as well as a speed choice?
choices: Caching makes every random value cryptographically secure
It forces all values to zero
It proves the original expression was deterministic
Reuse can retain previously computed values instead of recomputing new ones
questions.explanation: Persistence changes when results are reused. Be explicit about whether a stable snapshot or fresh evaluation is intended.

questions.prompt: Which observation most strongly suggests too little available parallelism?
choices: Many cores are idle while only a few long tasks remain
Every core is busy and all tasks finish together
questions.explanation: Few remaining tasks can limit resource utilization. Skew or a low partition count may explain the tail.

questions.prompt: Why is serialization size relevant to distributed performance?
choices: It affects transfer, storage and deserialization work
questions.explanation: Compact suitable representations can reduce network and memory costs, balanced against encoding CPU overhead.

questions.prompt: A tuning run changes data volume, partition count and cache state simultaneously. Why is its conclusion weak?
choices: The effect of each change cannot be isolated reliably
Spark requires exactly one column per benchmark
Every benchmark must run for an hour
Metrics are invalid whenever data is cached
questions.explanation: Controlled comparisons support causal conclusions. Change one main factor or design a deliberate experiment.

questions.prompt: What should determine whether a cache is retained across several pipeline phases?
choices: The alphabetical order of variable names
A rule that every DataFrame must be cached
Only the number of columns in the source schema
Measured reuse benefit versus storage pressure and recomputation cost
questions.explanation: Caching is a resource tradeoff. Remove data when its future benefit no longer justifies occupying storage.

questions.prompt: Which Spark reader constructs a streaming DataFrame?
questions.explanation: readStream creates a streaming source. The ordinary read interface constructs a batch DataFrame.

questions.prompt: What does isStreaming tell you about a DataFrame?
choices: Whether the query contains a streaming source
Whether every row is currently in memory
Whether a batch job has finished
questions.explanation: isStreaming identifies a streaming logical plan; it does not report query progress or storage residency.

questions.prompt: In a streaming event-time aggregation, which timestamp should represent when the business event happened?
choices: The driver's current wall-clock timestamp for every record
The time the notebook was opened
questions.explanation: Event time belongs to the event. Processing time describes when the system processes it; the distinction matters for delayed arrivals.

questions.prompt: What does a watermark primarily help Spark manage in a supported stateful query?
choices: How long certain event-time state must be retained
The maximum size of every input file
The number of columns in a schema
questions.explanation: Watermarks let supported operations retire state as event time advances. They are not a universal memory cap or a wall-clock timer.

questions.prompt: With a ten-minute watermark delay, which claim is safe for a supported aggregation?
choices: Data less late than the threshold is guaranteed not to be dropped by the watermark policy
Every event older than ten minutes is always dropped immediately
All windows close exactly ten wall-clock minutes after arrival
questions.explanation: The guarantee is one-sided. Data beyond the lateness threshold may or may not be processed; watermark progress depends on observed event time.

questions.prompt: Why should two independent streaming queries use different checkpoint directories?
choices: Each query needs its own recovery metadata and state
Checkpoints are ordinary CSV output folders
Sharing a directory automatically joins their data
Only the directory name determines watermark duration
questions.explanation: A checkpoint belongs to one query's recovery history. Sharing it between independent queries can corrupt or conflict with that history.

questions.prompt: What should you assume about a foreachBatch callback during recovery?
choices: A batch may be processed again, so external writes need an idempotency strategy
The callback cannot run more than once for a batch
Every external database automatically participates in Spark transactions
The batch ID is globally unique across unrelated queries
questions.explanation: foreachBatch provides at-least-once writes by default. Use the batch ID with a durable sink-specific deduplication or transaction design where appropriate.

questions.prompt: Which writeStream output mode emits only new final rows when the query supports it?
questions.explanation: Append emits newly added result rows. Stateful aggregations may require watermarks before rows are final enough to emit.

questions.prompt: Which streaming output mode sends the entire result table for each trigger when supported?
questions.explanation: Complete mode outputs the whole result table. It is different from batch overwrite mode and is not supported by every query or sink.

questions.prompt: What does awaitTermination() on a StreamingQuery normally do?
choices: Wait until the query terminates or an optional timeout expires
Convert the stream into a Python list
Force all late records into the next window
questions.explanation: awaitTermination lets a driver wait for query completion and can surface failures. It does not materialize an unbounded stream on the driver.

questions.prompt: Why is a fixed sleep after starting a streaming query a weak correctness test?
choices: Processing speed varies, so elapsed sleep does not prove expected output is committed
Sleep automatically advances every event-time watermark
A sleeping driver always drops every record
questions.explanation: Use observable query progress and deterministic input/output assertions with bounded waits. Wall-clock delay alone does not establish a processing boundary.

questions.prompt: What does the shape of this array report?
questions.code:

a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape)
questions.explanation: The outer sequence supplies two rows and each row contains three elements. Shape records the length of each axis.

questions.prompt: How does ndarray.ndim differ from ndarray.size?
choices: ndim counts bytes; size counts axes
ndim counts axes; size counts elements
questions.explanation: A shape of (2, 3, 4) has three axes and twenty-four elements. Neither property measures memory bytes directly.

questions.prompt: What is printed for this zero-dimensional array?
questions.code:

a = np.array(7)
print(a.ndim, a.size, a.shape)
questions.explanation: An array constructed from a scalar has zero axes but contains one element. It is different from a length-one vector.

questions.prompt: Which constructor directly creates a 4-by-2 array filled with -1?
questions.explanation: full sets every element to the supplied value. empty does not initialize numeric contents to that value.

questions.prompt: Why is np.empty unsafe as an array of zero counters before any initialization?
choices: It always creates a zero-length array
It guarantees every element is negative
questions.explanation: empty reserves storage without assigning meaningful numeric values. Initialize all entries before reading them.

questions.prompt: Which values does this half-open integer range contain?
questions.code:

print(np.arange(2, 11, 3).tolist())
questions.explanation: arange starts at two, advances by three, and excludes the stop value eleven.

questions.prompt: What is printed by this evenly spaced sample construction?
questions.code:

print(np.linspace(0, 1, 3).tolist())
questions.explanation: linspace takes a number of samples, not a step size. Its default endpoint=True includes both endpoints.

questions.prompt: Why should a binary exchange contract specify int32 or int64 rather than only 'int'?
choices: The string 'int' always means eight bits
The required width should not depend on platform defaults
questions.explanation: A concrete dtype makes storage width explicit. Endianness may also need to be part of a binary protocol.

questions.prompt: What values remain after this explicit integer-to-floating conversion?

print(a.astype(np.float64).tolist())

questions.prompt: A sensor counter can exceed 255. Why is uint8 unsuitable without an overflow policy?
choices: It automatically grows into uint64 on every assignment
It has a bounded representable range
questions.explanation: uint8 represents zero through 255. Fixed-width numeric arithmetic and conversion require deliberate overflow handling.

questions.prompt: What does this array report for its element-storage bytes?
questions.code:

a = np.zeros((2, 3), dtype=np.int32)
print(a.nbytes)
questions.explanation: There are six elements at four bytes each. nbytes describes element storage, not all Python object overhead.

questions.prompt: What is a key consequence of using dtype=object for numeric records?
choices: All nested objects are deeply copied
Elements hold Python object references and many numeric optimizations are lost
Every object is stored as a fixed-width float
questions.explanation: Object arrays can hold heterogeneous Python values, but they do not provide the same compact native numeric representation.

questions.prompt: Which shape has the same element count as an array of shape (3, 4)?
questions.explanation: The product of dimensions must match: both (3, 4) and (2, 6) contain twelve elements.

questions.prompt: A float array is cast to int64. For finite values within range, how are fractional parts handled?
choices: They are always rounded to the nearest even integer
They cause an exception in every case
They are retained as hidden metadata
questions.explanation: A numeric integer cast truncates finite in-range floating values. Use an explicit rounding operation first if a different policy is intended.

questions.prompt: Which dtype is most appropriate for a simple validity mask?
questions.explanation: Boolean arrays represent true/false conditions and participate directly in Boolean indexing.

questions.prompt: What is printed after explicitly creating an empty two-dimensional batch?
questions.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.empty((0, 3), dtype=np.float64)
print(a.shape, a.size)
questions.explanation: A dimension of length zero makes the total size zero while the other axis still records the expected column count.

questions.prompt: Why should identifiers with leading zeros usually remain textual rather than be cast to integers?
choices: Numeric conversion loses representation that may carry business meaning
NumPy cannot store integers larger than nine
Integer conversion always preserves original formatting
questions.explanation: An identifier is not necessarily a quantity. Converting '0012' to an integer discards its leading zeros.

questions.prompt: A fixed-width Unicode array has dtype '<U3'. What is a risk when assigning a longer string?
choices: The dtype always expands in place
The array automatically becomes a Python list
The assignment necessarily adds a new axis
The value can be truncated to the dtype's character capacity

questions.prompt: What is the type relationship between a Python list and a NumPy ndarray?
choices: An ndarray is only a synonym for list
Every ndarray must have two axes
An ndarray has array metadata and a dtype; a list is a general Python container
A list always stores one contiguous native numeric dtype
questions.explanation: NumPy arrays add typed element storage and multidimensional metadata. Python lists can reference arbitrary objects.

questions.prompt: For a precise requested number of floating-point samples, why is linspace often clearer than arange with a fractional step?
choices: linspace guarantees no rounding error in every sample
The sample count is explicit and avoids step-accumulation surprises
questions.explanation: Floating-point steps can produce surprising endpoints or counts. linspace specifies the intended count but still uses floating-point representation.

questions.prompt: What is selected by this two-axis position?
questions.code:

print(int(a[1, 2]))
questions.explanation: The first index selects the second row, and the second selects its third element. NumPy indexes are zero-based.

questions.prompt: What shape does selecting this single column produce?
questions.code:

a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a[:, 1].shape)
questions.explanation: An integer index removes the selected axis. Use a column slice such as 1:2 to retain a length-one column axis.

questions.prompt: What shape does this column slice preserve?
questions.code:

a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)
print(a[:, 1:2].shape)
questions.explanation: A slice retains its axis, even when the slice contains only one column.

questions.prompt: Which expression reverses a one-dimensional array without requesting a gathered integer-index copy?
questions.explanation: A slice with step -1 traverses the elements backward. A zero step is invalid and a[-1] selects only the final element.

questions.prompt: Which values survive this Boolean selection?
questions.code:

questions.prompt: Why does '(a > 0) and (a < 10)' fail for a multi-element ndarray?
choices: and always selects only the first row
The array must be transposed first
and requires a scalar truth value, which is ambiguous for the array

questions.prompt: Which expression selects values strictly between zero and ten?
questions.explanation: Parenthesized comparisons joined with & express intersection. The OR condition accepts values outside the intended interval.

questions.prompt: What values result from paired advanced indexes here?

print(a[[0, 2], [1, 3]].tolist())

questions.prompt: Which selection explicitly forms the Cartesian product of row indexes [0, 2] and column indexes [1, 3]?
questions.explanation: ix_ creates broadcastable index grids so both selected columns are obtained for each selected row.

questions.prompt: What remains in a after mutating this gathered selection?

b[0] = 99

questions.prompt: What does this direct advanced-index assignment do?

a[[0, 2]] = 99
print(a.tolist())
choices: It raises because advanced indexing never supports assignment
questions.explanation: Direct indexed assignment targets the original array. This differs from retrieving a gathered copy and modifying that separate result.

questions.prompt: A row mask for an array with shape (5, 3) has length four. What should happen with a[mask]?
choices: The array is padded with a zero row
An indexing error due to incompatible mask length
The mask repeats automatically to five rows
The unmatched row is silently discarded

questions.prompt: What does a[-1] select from a nonempty one-dimensional array?

questions.prompt: What is the effect of adding None in this index?

choices: The array is converted to object dtype
A new row filled with zeros is appended
A new length-one axis is inserted

questions.prompt: In a[..., 0], what does the ellipsis stand for?
choices: Enough full slices to cover the unspecified leading axes

questions.prompt: Why can a[[0, 0]] += 1 increment a[0] only once rather than twice?
choices: The array becomes immutable after one update
Advanced indexing uses buffered gather-and-write behavior
NumPy removes every zero index before arithmetic
Integer increments are nondeterministic by design

questions.prompt: What does unbuffered repeated-index accumulation print?

questions.prompt: When a two-dimensional Boolean mask has the same shape as a, what shape does a[mask] normally have?
choices: A scalar regardless of selected count
A matrix with one column per true value
A one-dimensional array of selected elements

questions.prompt: Which operation retrieves the positions where a one-dimensional mask is true?

questions.prompt: A pipeline requires a selected subset that can be edited without affecting its source. Which explicit approach makes that intent clear for a basic slice?

questions.prompt: Which rule determines whether two axis lengths are broadcast-compatible?
choices: They are equal or one of them is one
The left length must be larger
questions.explanation: Broadcasting compares trailing dimensions. Equal lengths or a length-one dimension can align without requiring identical full shapes.

questions.prompt: What is the result of adding this feature offset to every row?

questions.prompt: What output shape results from adding arrays of shape (4, 1) and (1, 6)?
questions.explanation: Each length-one dimension expands against the corresponding non-one dimension, yielding a four-by-six result.

questions.prompt: Why are shapes (5, 3) and (5,) incompatible for elementwise addition?
choices: Five rows exceed a NumPy limit
Their trailing dimensions compare as three and five
Broadcasting always compares only the first dimension
A vector cannot be added to a matrix

questions.prompt: What does the multiplication operator do between two compatible ndarrays?
questions.explanation: The * operator is elementwise for ndarrays. Matrix multiplication uses @ or matmul.

questions.prompt: Which shape should per-row weights have to multiply a feature matrix of shape (n, p) independently of whether n equals p?
questions.explanation: A length-one trailing axis allows each row weight to broadcast across the p features. A flat (n,) vector aligns to columns instead.

questions.prompt: What values does this elementwise conditional selection produce?

questions.prompt: Why does np.where(den != 0, num / den, 0) not necessarily suppress divide-by-zero warnings?

The division expression is evaluated before where selects values
questions.explanation: Python evaluates the branch arrays before calling where. Use the ufunc's where argument with an initialized out array for masked division.

questions.prompt: A Python function wrapped with np.vectorize remains slow. Which explanation is most accurate?
choices: vectorize guarantees a native SIMD implementation
All vectorized-looking code has identical speed
vectorize is mainly a convenience wrapper, not a general performance compiler
vectorize distributes work over a Spark cluster
questions.explanation: The wrapper can still call Python code per element. Prefer native array operations or benchmark an appropriate compiled implementation.

questions.prompt: What does clipping this array to the inclusive interval [0, 5] produce?

questions.prompt: What does the out argument of a compatible NumPy ufunc let a caller control?
choices: The destination array for the result
The location of a checkpoint directory
The final sort order of rows
questions.explanation: out can reuse allocated storage when shapes and casting rules permit it. It does not eliminate every possible temporary or change mathematical semantics.

questions.prompt: Why can an all-pairs distance calculation exhaust memory despite using broadcasting?

The smaller input must always be copied a million times
Broadcasting always serializes each value to JSON
The broadcasted result or intermediate can have the full pairwise size

questions.prompt: Why is explicitly tiling a per-feature vector often unnecessary before adding it to a matrix?

questions.prompt: What does this ufunc pipeline calculate?

questions.prompt: Why can a += 0.5 fail when a is an integer ndarray even though a + 0.5 succeeds?

questions.prompt: For two equal-length one-dimensional arrays, what does np.einsum('i,i->', a, b) express?

questions.prompt: What values does multiplying an integer ndarray by a scalar produce?

questions.prompt: What does a.sum() do when axis is omitted for a numeric ndarray?
choices: Sums all elements into a scalar result
Returns a running total for every element

questions.prompt: What sequence does this cumulative sum return?

questions.prompt: What does this argmax return?

questions.prompt: Why might dtype=np.float64 be supplied when averaging float32 measurements?

To use a higher-precision accumulator for the mean
questions.explanation: A wider accumulator can reduce rounding error. It does not make arbitrary floating-point results exact or define a missing-value policy.

questions.prompt: What does explicitly choosing an int64 accumulator protect against when summing many int16 counts?
choices: Overflow in a narrow accumulator, within int64's remaining range
All possible integer overflow regardless of total
questions.explanation: The chosen accumulator widens arithmetic capacity. Its own finite range must still be respected.

questions.prompt: Which scalar condition asks whether at least one element of mask is true?

questions.prompt: Which expression centers each row of a two-dimensional floating array?

questions.prompt: For shape (2, 3, 4), what shape remains after sum(axis=(0, 2))?

questions.prompt: How does ddof=1 change the denominator in variance relative to ddof=0?

questions.prompt: What population variance is printed for these two values?

questions.prompt: A distributed pipeline sums floats in a different grouping after repartitioning. Why can its final low-order bits differ?
choices: Floating-point values are exact decimal numbers
Floating-point addition is not generally associative
Every repartition changes business values intentionally

questions.prompt: What does np.maximum.reduce(a) compute for a nonempty one-dimensional numeric array?

questions.prompt: What identity result does summing an empty integer array normally produce?

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to interpret a zero aggregate as proof that a batch contained data?

An empty sum can also be zero

questions.prompt: A metric array may be empty. What should happen before calling argmax?
choices: Pad the array with a random value
Convert it to bool and ignore its length
Handle the empty case explicitly under a business rule

questions.prompt: What is the median of these values?

questions.prompt: What shape is inferred for the -1 dimension?

questions.prompt: Which claim about np.reshape is correct?

It returns a view when possible and a copy otherwise
It always returns a view regardless of strides
questions.explanation: A reshape must preserve element count, and the input layout determines whether a metadata-only view can express the requested shape.

questions.prompt: How does flatten differ from ravel regarding copies?
choices: flatten always copies; ravel copies only when necessary
ravel always copies; flatten never copies
Neither can create a one-dimensional result

questions.prompt: What remains in a after this flatten result is changed?

questions.prompt: What shape does transposing a one-dimensional array produce?

questions.prompt: Which function can check whether two ndarrays actually overlap in element storage?

questions.prompt: Why can keeping a tiny slice alive retain a very large allocation?

Every slice serializes the full array to disk
A view always duplicates the complete array
NumPy automatically rounds every slice to a gigabyte

questions.prompt: What does np.ascontiguousarray(a) guarantee for its returned ndarray?

questions.prompt: Which source position changes through this transpose view?

questions.prompt: Does copying an object-dtype array necessarily clone the mutable Python objects it references?
choices: No, because object arrays cannot be copied at all
No, the contained object references can still point to shared objects
Yes, every nested object is recursively cloned
Yes, but only when there are two axes
questions.explanation: An array copy duplicates its element storage, which for object dtype contains references. Recursive object copying is a separate operation.

questions.prompt: What is printed for the sharing relationships in this example?

The view automatically caches every sum
